## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

A cycle's record has one home at a time, and while the cycle runs this is it. At Preparation
the picked-up `## Todo` item **moves** here (never copied, one home per text) and becomes six
provisional items, all required, all revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block moves
into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` and becomes that cycle's `##` section. It is never written in
two places. Shape:

```
### <type>: <title>

#### Problem
<what is wrong, a sentence or two>

#### Solution
<what will be done about it, broad; provisional until the close-out>

#### Acceptance check
<the measure of "are you finished?">

#### Ladder
- <title> opening (done)
- <title> (current)
- <title>
- <close-out title>

#### Deliberation
<how the five above were decided; `_None._` if there was nothing to deliberate>

#### Ladder details
<optional: one `#####` subsection per rung with conceptual content, headed by its exact title>
```

A multi-cycle program adds one level: the program is the `###`, its current cycle the `####`,
and the six items sit one level below that (headings give the current work durable anchors,
which numbered Todo entries can't). Full rules in
[cycle-protocol.md](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#preparation); the move's four transforms are
in [Chores sections](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

### docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd

#### Problem

Both repos' `.vc-config.toml` carry a fossil `[push]` comment block from an older binary's
schema, the retired `.vc-x1` state dirs linger (empty dirs on disk, a `/.vc-x1` line in the
work `.gitignore`), generated config comments have no refresh tooling so they rot silently, and
the bot dir's `.claude` name is agent-specific where this workspace wants the neutral
`.agent-session`.

#### Solution

# custom-family.md - vc-x1's layer, as a member of the vc-x1 agent-file family

Read after [custom.md](custom.md), whose single convention entry points here. Present only in a
member repo. A project that is not a member does not carry this file, and nothing in it applies
to one.

**A member's `custom.md` differs from the payload by that one line, and everything of its own lives
here.** That is the family's convention and it buys a property worth having: `diff custom.md
<template>/work/custom.md` is one line for every member, so the file that can never be pinned still
converges, and a member's whole customization surface is this file. The medium below is here for
that reason rather than because it has anything to do with the family.

## Medium and validation

The artifact is the `vc-x1` CLI, a Rust crate (manifest `Cargo.toml`, package name `vc-x1`).
Versioning specifics are in [versioning.md](agent-data/versioning.md).

**What a version bump promises**: `X.Y.Z` is a scope signal to readers of the history (see
[Advancing X.Y.Z](agent-data/versioning.md#advancing-xyz-scope-decides)), not a compatibility
contract. The crate has no library target, but the built CLI has external consumers (the family's
repos run it), so a change that breaks an existing invocation or the `.vc-config.toml` schema is
called out in the commit and surfaced by the tool's own errors rather than promised by the
version. Revisit with a compat clause if a library crate ever splits out.

**Single-name convention** (adopted at the 0.78.3 cycle): the package name is the binary's
name, `vc-x1` on `main`, with per-line dev names on long-lived branches, guarded by `build.rs`
on every cargo verb. This is the project's answer to versioning.md's
[Dev artifact name](agent-data/versioning.md#dev-artifact-name): the repo is striving to
release, so `main` builds install as plain `vc-x1`.

- **Full validation**
  - when: per-commit checklist step 5 (skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out)
  - run as separate invocations, each exit status checked:
    1. `cargo fmt`
    2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
    3. `cargo test`
    4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
    5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
- **Fast validation**
  - when: ladder checklist step 3
  - `cargo test --bins`

## Membership

- **member name**: `vc-x1`
- **template repository**: `../vc-x1-template`

These two are environment rather than instruction, the same species as `.vc-config.toml`'s
`[repos]` paths, and they belong there instead. They cannot move yet: `vc-x1 config --validate`
rejects keys it does not know, so a config carrying them would fail its own validator. The
`[private]` table proposal tracks the fix.

## Messaging

Members leave word for each other in per-member mailboxes at the template repository. The protocol
is `../vc-x1-template/MESSAGES.md` and it governs. These are the parts that decide how a session
behaves.

- **At acquaint, check `../vc-x1-template/messages/vc-x1.md`.** An absent file means no mail.
- **Handle, then delete** the entry, and delete the file once it empties. Mailboxes hold open
  items only.
- **So a message can never be a record.** Anything in one worth keeping is copied into
  `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` *before* the entry is deleted.
- **Messages are thin pointers, not state.** Durable coordination state lives in topical files. A
  message says "action needed, see <file>" rather than restating the details.
- **Write to a member's mailbox, never into their repo.** A repo with a live session is written
  only by its own agent.

## Dogfood log

This project's log lives in [notes/dogfood.md](notes/dogfood.md): dated entries on where the
pinned instructions chafed, failed, or got amended, the evidence base for the family's
convergence decisions ([Changing the agent-files](AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)). It stays
a separate file because it predates this one and is long. In-flight entries only: a resolved
entry retires at the beat where it resolves, per
[Retiring Done entries](agent-data/notes.md#retiring-done-entries).

59	#### Solution
60	
61	Make a repo-root `vc-config.toml` prototype the schema's single source, then rebuild the
62	config surface from it:
63	
64	- the prototype holds real TOML tables, one per settable key: doc, used-by, default,
65	  reference url
66	- build.rs parses it and generates the schema table and default constants
67	  - `src/config_schema.rs` shrinks to the include plus hand-written helpers
68	  - behavioral defaults (col-width, result-lines) consume the generated constants, so the
69	    code cannot disagree with the file
70	- regenerate both config files from that pipeline, retiring the fossil comment blocks
71	- retire the state-dir leftovers
72	- add a `config --refresh` that rewrites a file's commented schema block while preserving
73	  active keys and `[repos]`
74	  - a `--check` mode renders and compares without writing, exiting nonzero on any
75	    difference, so a prototype edit that skipped the refresh fails loudly
76	- add a `validate-anchors` subcommand, the validate-repo design's first standalone slice:
77	  same-file heading anchors checked via the documented slug algorithm, plus `[N]` reference
78	  resolution, across the repo's markdown records
79	- repoint `repos.bot` at `.agent-session`
80	  - the directory rename itself is wink's move between sessions (a live session writes
81	    through the symlink), with the following session committing the record
82	
83	#### Acceptance check
84	
85	1. build.rs generates the schema table and default constants from `vc-config.toml`
86	   (rerun-if-changed wired), the hand-kept `COL_WIDTH` / `RESULT_LINE_CAP` constants are gone
87	   from `src/`, and generated configs carry each key's `reference:` line.
88	2. `vc-x1 config --validate` is clean on both sides, and neither file mentions `[push]`,
89	   `state-dir`, or `state-file`.
90	3. `config --refresh` on a fixture with stale comment blocks and active keys preserves the
91	   active keys and `[repos]` while replacing the stale blocks (a test demonstrates it).
92	4. `config --refresh --check` exits clean on both sides, proving the committed config files
93	   match what the prototype renders.
94	5. After the rename: `repos.bot = ".agent-session"`, a cycle rung pushes from a session end to
95	   end, and new commits still stamp `/.claude/`-labeled ochid trailers.
96	6. No `.vc-x1` dir in either repo and no `/.vc-x1` line in `.gitignore`, which ignores the bot
97	   dir under its new name.
98	7. `validate-anchors` runs clean over `TODO.md`, `notes/`, `README.md`, and `vc-config.md`
99	   (same-file heading anchors and `[N]` refs), and a test shows it catching a broken anchor.
100	
101	#### Ladder
102	
103	- docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd opening (done)
104	- docs: separate work review stop (done)
105	- feat: vc-config.toml prototype + build.rs codegen (done)
106	- docs: ladder ToC + per-rung sections (done)
107	- chore: regenerate stale config files (next)
108	- feat: add config --refresh
109	- feat: add validate-anchors
110	- docs: vc-config.md per-key examples
111	- chore: point config at .agent-session
112	- docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd
113	
114	#### Deliberation
115	
116	- the `.agent-session` rename was leaning toward its own cycle; it folds in here because it
117	  needs an inter-session quiesce, which a multi-step cycle's `/exit` between rungs naturally
118	  provides
119	- the ochid prefix is a canonical side label decoupled from the bot dir's path (test-pinned: a
120	  custom bot dir still stamps `/.claude/`), so history and future trailers stay coherent across
121	  the rename
122	- pinned files name `.claude` as the bot repo's path; the rename step updates that text to
123	  path-neutral wording as a family proposal, this member's diff carrying it until convergence
124	- 0.79.0 is spoken for by the trapezoid branch's anticipated close-out, so this cycle is a
125	  patch at 0.78.8
126	- the close-out title dropped ".toml" from wink's phrasing so the opening bookend stays inside

- the prototype holds real TOML tables, one per settable key: doc, used-by, default,
  reference url
- build.rs parses it and generates the schema table and default constants
  - `src/config_schema.rs` shrinks to the include plus hand-written helpers
  - behavioral defaults (col-width, result-lines) consume the generated constants, so the
    code cannot disagree with the file
- regenerate both config files from that pipeline, retiring the fossil comment blocks
- retire the state-dir leftovers
- add a `config --refresh` that rewrites a file's commented schema block while preserving
  active keys and `[repos]`
  - a `--check` mode renders and compares without writing, exiting nonzero on any
    difference, so a prototype edit that skipped the refresh fails loudly
- add a `validate-anchors` subcommand, the validate-repo design's first standalone slice:
  same-file heading anchors checked via the documented slug algorithm, plus `[N]` reference
  resolution, across the repo's markdown records

    through the symlink), with the following session committing the record

## 2026-08-03 from iiac-perf (f5) + wink: adopt jj revsets (docs + CLI), mailbox config, 3 fixes

iiac-perf's review of the 20260803 baseline, plus two items from wink's session with it today;
the rest of the review (drop-list verdict, adoption sequencing, tier-2 views) lands at today's
discussion. The headline is a decision wink made today, not yet discussed with you: the
family's house revset convention was a mistake, and jj's native semantics should be adopted,
docs and CLI both, ASAP.

- **Adopt jj's revset semantics; retire the house convention** (wink, 2026-08-03)
  - the trigger: jj.md's new Revsets primer and jj-tips.md gloss `X..` as "descendants of X
    excluding X"; in jj itself `x..` is `~::x` (everything not an ancestor of x), which on a
    repo with parked branches includes unrelated commits. The primer documents raw `-r`
    arguments, so the gloss feeds real `jj rebase` / `jj abandon` target choices
  - the CLI: vc-x1 currently converts house-convention revsets to jj's when issuing jj
    commands; it should stop converting and pass revsets to jj verbatim, so one dialect
    exists and `jj help -k revsets` is the single authority
  - cutover care: the two dialects share syntax, so the flip is silent; sweep the repos'
    durable text for `..`-form revsets in the same cycle. iiac-perf's protocol usages are all
    `..@`, which means the same thing in both dialects, so its sweep is small; jj-tips.md's
    tutorial transcripts (~lines 282-289, 334-337) are the real rewrites
  - docs rewrite: teach `::` as the primary, symmetric operator (`::x` ancestors, `x::`
    descendants, `x::y` the path); present `..` as git-compatible set subtraction with a
    warning on the open-ended forms; add one history line noting vc-x1 formerly translated a
    house convention, so old transcripts stay decodable
- **Mailbox parameters belong in `.vc-config.toml`, not custom.md** (from wink's
  byte-identical-instruction-files goal, 2026-08-03; a discussion item, not a decision)
  - the goal: custom.md generic at birth, so a new repo is byte-identical to the payload from
    its first commit and any later diff is a real customization
  - the blocker: custom.md currently carries the member name and the template repository's
    path, and AGENTS.md's acquaint-time practice depends on both
  - the fix: those are environment configuration, not instruction text, and `.vc-config.toml`
    already holds that species of fact (`other-repo = ".claude"`, a per-checkout relative
    path) while sitting outside the pinned set, so moving them costs byte-identity nothing
  - the pinned practice then assumes no layout: check your mailbox at acquaint if this project
    participates in a message community, whose location and your member name come from
    `.vc-config.toml`; absent config means no community, a free no-op. Non-participation
    becomes the silent default rather than an override, which is backwards today
  - why layout-free matters (wink): the sibling arrangement of the family's repos is a local
    convention, not something an outside adopter should inherit, nor one we are committed to
    keeping. iiac-perf's earlier suggestion to pin it as a family-wide rule is withdrawn
- **custom.md skeleton: stale validation step number**: work/custom.md points Full validation
  at "per-commit checklist step 4", but the renumbered checklist has "Close the records" at 4
  and validation at 5
- **prose.md: two lines over its own <=100 limit**: line 19 (106 cols) and line 71 (134 cols),
  both from the 0802/0803 amendment splices; a rewrap fixes both
- **versioning.md: "this project" narration in a pinned file**: "This project adopted the
  convention 2026-07-23 (during 0.75.0)" reads as the reader's own history; name vc-x1 or
  drop the sentence (the vc-x1-dev example itself is fine as an example)

- **Adopt jj's revset semantics; retire the house convention** (wink, 2026-08-03)
  - the trigger: jj.md's new Revsets primer and jj-tips.md gloss `X..` as "descendants of X
    excluding X"; in jj itself `x..` is `~::x` (everything not an ancestor of x), which on a
    repo with parked branches includes unrelated commits. The primer documents raw `-r`
    arguments, so the gloss feeds real `jj rebase` / `jj abandon` target choices
  - the CLI: vc-x1 currently converts house-convention revsets to jj's when issuing jj
    commands; it should stop converting and pass revsets to jj verbatim, so one dialect
    exists and `jj help -k revsets` is the single authority
  - cutover care: the two dialects share syntax, so the flip is silent; sweep the repos'
    durable text for `..`-form revsets in the same cycle. iiac-perf's protocol usages are all
    `..@`, which means the same thing in both dialects, so its sweep is small; jj-tips.md's
    tutorial transcripts (~lines 282-289, 334-337) are the real rewrites
  - docs rewrite: teach `::` as the primary, symmetric operator (`::x` ancestors, `x::`
    descendants, `x::y` the path); present `..` as git-compatible set subtraction with a
    warning on the open-ended forms; add one history line noting vc-x1 formerly translated a
    house convention, so old transcripts stay decodable
- **Mailbox parameters belong in `.vc-config.toml`, not custom.md** (from wink's
  byte-identical-instruction-files goal, 2026-08-03; a discussion item, not a decision)
  - the goal: custom.md generic at birth, so a new repo is byte-identical to the payload from
    its first commit and any later diff is a real customization
  - the blocker: custom.md currently carries the member name and the template repository's
    path, and AGENTS.md's acquaint-time practice depends on both
  - the fix: those are environment configuration, not instruction text, and `.vc-config.toml`
    already holds that species of fact (`other-repo = ".claude"`, a per-checkout relative
    path) while sitting outside the pinned set, so moving them costs byte-identity nothing
  - the pinned practice then assumes no layout: check your mailbox at acquaint if this project
    participates in a message community, whose location and your member name come from
    `.vc-config.toml`; absent config means no community, a free no-op. Non-participation
    becomes the silent default rather than an override, which is backwards today
  - why layout-free matters (wink): the sibling arrangement of the family's repos is a local
    convention, not something an outside adopter should inherit, nor one we are committed to
    keeping. iiac-perf's earlier suggestion to pin it as a family-wide rule is withdrawn
- **custom.md skeleton: stale validation step number**: work/custom.md points Full validation
  at "per-commit checklist step 4", but the renumbered checklist has "Close the records" at 4
  and validation at 5
- **prose.md: two lines over its own <=100 limit**: line 19 (106 cols) and line 71 (134 cols),

- **versioning.md: "this project" narration in a pinned file**: "This project adopted the
  convention 2026-07-23 (during 0.75.0)" reads as the reader's own history; name vc-x1 or
  drop the sentence (the vc-x1-dev example itself is fine as an example)

Done when: the docs fixes land in the template payload (jj-tips.md included for the revset
item), the CLI's revset pass-through is tracked vc-x1-side (its cycle is yours to scope), and
the mailbox-config move has your view on the schema, which it needs before the pinned practice
can be reworded.

## 2026-07-31 from wink + iiac-perf (f5): template restructure landed; old repos await your discussion

`vc-x1-template` (this repo) is the new template + coordination point: payload split into
`work/` + `work.claude/` so init copies only payload (the old flat layout copied discussion
files into new repos; see public exhibit https://github.com/winksaville/test1). Invocation:
`vc-x1 init <name> --use-template <path>/vc-x1-template/work` (single arg; the `<CODE>.claude`
concat default finds `work.claude/`).

- disposition of `vc-x1-work-repo-template` (+ its `.claude`) and `vc-x1-bot-repo-template` is
  deliberately untouched, pending wink discussing it with you; their working copies were left
  exactly as found
- CLI ideas triaged 2026-08-02 into vc-x1's `notes/todo-backlog.md` #46 ("init template
  ergonomics"); the remaining open item is the old repos' fate

Done when: you and wink have decided the old repos' fate.

1	# Cycle checklists
2	
3	Checklists for the moments where slips happen: committing, pushing, closing out. The full
4	protocol, with rationale and recovery procedures, is
5	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md). On any disagreement, that file wins. Re-read
6	the relevant checklist immediately before the action. Don't run it from memory.
7	
8	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
9	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
10	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
11	
12	## The cycle at a glance
13	
14	Every change runs as a **cycle** with three phases: Preparation -> Work -> Close-out. The
15	phases always happen, but there are two styles. A **multi-step** cycle commits them
16	individually, as a ladder of steps (the Preparation commit is optional); a
17	**single-step** cycle folds all three into one commit when the change is straightforward, so
18	that one commit is the close-out and carries its duties, mandatory validation included. The
19	ladder lists a cycle's steps in order and identifies each by its title, with no number and no
20	version. Where the version-of-record lives and how often it is bumped are in
21	[versioning.md](versioning.md). Read [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md) before any commit
22	work, and before any push, cycle or not.
23	
24	## Cycles run on a bookmark
25	
26	A cycle runs on its own topic bookmark, created at the opening and named for the cycle. `main`
27	advances only by landing one. Nothing pushes straight to `main`.
28	
29	- **The bookmark is the unit of review.** Everything the cycle does is visible as one line
30	  against `main`, and until it lands the whole line is a draft that can be reshaped
31	  ([Topic bookmarks are drafts](#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts)). Landing is the single approval
32	  that makes the cycle permanent.
33	- **Create at the opening**, land at the close-out. Commands are in
34	  [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land), and the opening's other duties are in
35	  the [Opening checklist](#opening-checklist) below.
36	- **A single-step cycle still gets one.** The saving is not worth the exception, and a
37	  one-commit line is exactly the case where a pre-landing rewrite is cheapest.
38	- **The permanent branch is whatever this project calls it** (`main` here). A long-lived program
39	  bookmark is a different animal, governed by
40	  [Long-lived bookmarks](jj.md#long-lived-bookmarks-merge-only-by-default-deletable-once-merged).
41	
42	**Why:** a cycle that pushes `main` directly makes every correction a coordinated force-push of
43	published history. Landing costs one command and buys free rewrites for the whole cycle.
44	
45	## Opening checklist
46	
47	At the cycle's opening, before the first Work commit:
48	
49	1. Create the cycle's bookmark ([Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land)).
50	2. Move the picked-up item into `TODO.md > ## In Progress` and write the **six provisional
51	   items** there, all six required. The title is a heading one level below `## In Progress`'s
52	   own level, and the other five are headings one level below the title (a plain cycle: `###`
53	   title, `####` items; under a program heading, each one deeper):
54	   - **title**, which becomes the chores section header at close-out
55	   - **problem statement**: what is wrong, a sentence or two
56	   - **solution statement**: what will be done about it, broad
57	   - **acceptance check**: the measure of "are you finished?"
58	   - **ladder**: one rung per step, bare title plus `(current)` / `(done)`
59	   - **deliberation**: how the five above were decided (`_None._` when there was nothing to
60	     deliberate)
61	   A `Ladder details` area may follow the six as rungs complete, one subsection per rung with
62	   conceptual content, headed by the rung's exact title (see the protocol's
63	   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)).
64	3. Sweep `## Done` per [Retiring Done entries](notes.md#retiring-done-entries), then bump the
65	   version-of-record.
66	
67	Nothing is opened in the chores file here. The block is the cycle's only home until close-out
68	moves it. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).
69	
70	**Why the acceptance check:** a cycle's own checklists are per-commit instruments and every one
71	of them can pass while the banner claim is false. Measured in a seven-cycle program opened
72	against "end subprocess spawning": its close-out claimed the goal met, with about twenty spawn
73	sites surviving, two inside the facade the program built. A measurement or performance claim is
74	the shape most exposed, since "we measured it" is easy to believe and hard to notice you have not
75	done. Being provisional, the check can also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
76	same failure by a slower route. A changed check is one of the things the deliberation justifies.
77	
78	## Committing vs pushing
79	
80	A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`. Never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
81	commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
82	`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). A
83	pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate. In
84	an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
85	is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
86	publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
87	around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
88	cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).
89	
90	## Topic bookmarks are drafts
91	
92	A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch. Pushed there is not published.
93	So keep the series inside it self-consistent: inserting or reordering a step edits the ladder in
94	the rungs that already committed an older version of it, not only at the tip.
95	
96	- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
97	  `jj describe`, so hard rule 4 stays intact and the `ochid:` trailers ride along untouched
98	  (they carry change ids, which survive a rewrite).
99	- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
100	- **Exceptions, where self-consistency is not worth its cost**: the bookmark has already landed;
101	  another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or the ladder
102	  is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.
103	
104	The squash-form ladder below never meets this, since nothing on it is pushed. The rule is for the
105	multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time. Full statement in the protocol's
106	[Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).
107	
108	## Per-commit checklist
109	
110	Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
111	[Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):
112	
113	1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
114	2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
115	3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit, and write the rung's
116	   `Ladder details` subsection when it has conceptual content (exact title as its heading; the
117	   ladder itself stays a bare ToC). See the protocol's
118	   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation).
119	4. Bump the version-of-record to this commit's version (the suffix scheme is in
120	   [versioning.md](versioning.md)). The opening checklist's bump already covers a Preparation
121	   commit.
122	5. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
123	   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
124	6. Stop and ask the user, "please review", as this is the bottom of the review loop. Do not present
125	   a description as we iterate until the user reviews and says "continue|go|.." indicating the work
126	   review is likely complete.
127	7. Once the work review is complete, write the description: a conventional title, then a problem
128	   statement and a solution statement, both broad, sized per prose.md's
129	   [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths). No version in either, no file list (the diff is the
130	   mechanical record), and no deliberation (chores, todo, and the session hold that). See
131	   [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
132	8. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
133	   explicitly includes it.
134	9. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
135	   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.
136	
137	## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist
138	
139	Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
140	[per-Work-commit contract](cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):
141	
142	1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
143	2. Do the commit's work.
144	3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
145	4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
146	   the one permitted describe. The commit is never published and never carries a trailer.
147	
148	Nothing on a ladder is pushed. The close-out squash
149	(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
150	publishes the single commit.
151	
152	## Before any push
153	
154	- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
155	  is not push approval. "Commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
156	  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
157	  bounded task only. Destructive ops still pause.
158	- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
159	- Closing words are already written. Nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).
160	
161	## After the final push: hard stop
162	
163	Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
164	verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
165	words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token
166	after the tool returns. If so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
167	or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
168	delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps; the hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
169	push. See
170	[After push or squash-push](cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).
171	
172	## Close-out checklist
173	
174	The cycle's last step, per the protocol's
175	[Close-out](cycle-protocol.md#close-out):
176	
177	1. **Run the acceptance check** the opening stated, and record what it showed in the
178	   `## In Progress` block, whether or not it passed. A check that was never run is a failed
179	   close-out, and a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to quietly restate the banner.
180	2. **Finalize the six items in place**: sync the title if the scope shifted, replace the
181	   provisional solution statement with what was done, drop the ladder's `(current)` / `(done)`
182	   markers, add any design subsections.
183	3. **Move the block** into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, which is what creates the section.
184	   Four transforms, two of which fail silently: headings one level deeper, rung refs renumbered
185	   into the destination's namespace, repo-root-relative links gain `../`, forward-looking notes
186	   rewritten. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). Add the title-only
187	   `## Table of Contents` entry.
188	4. Write the `## Done` entry: the version, then a bold title line with its chores `[N]` ref,
189	   detail as sub-bullets (see [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)). Replace the
190	   `## In Progress` block with `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
191	5. Full validation, mandatory.
192	6. Update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
193	7. At push time, surface the shape options (squash / trapezoid / keep separate) and wait for
194	   the user's choice. The trapezoid recipe is
195	   [in the protocol](cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe). Its step 4 is
196	   `jj git push`, not `vc-x1 push`.
197	8. **Land the bookmark** on the user's go. Until this, nothing the cycle pushed is permanent. See
198	   [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land).
199	9. Backfill the chores as-built ladder refs (and any remaining legacy `Commits:` lines) for the
200	   commits landing just made permanent, which is the whole cycle rather than the previous push's
201	   share. Never record a SHA that is not on a permanent branch. The backfill edits ride the next
202	   push (a commit cannot record its own SHA).
203	
204	## vc-x1 push behaviors to keep in mind
205	
206	Three, independent of project language:
207	
208	- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents beyond
209	  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, and runs no build or tests. The medium's validation is the
210	  per-commit flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`. The one check that remains is
211	  `push-work` verifying the bookmark's remote refs are tracked, which is its own precondition.
212	- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume. Every stage no-ops when its
213	  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If a run fails, push stops and
214	  reports. Getting the repos back to a sensible state is the user's call, not something the
215	  tool infers.
216	- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself, so don't hand-write them into the
217	  commit body or `--title`/`--body`.

   - **deliberation**: how the five above were decided (`_None._` when there was nothing to
     deliberate)
   A `Ladder details` area may follow the six as rungs complete, one subsection per rung with
   conceptual content, headed by the rung's exact title (see the protocol's
   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation)).
3. Sweep `## Done` per [Retiring Done entries](notes.md#retiring-done-entries), then bump the
   version-of-record.

Nothing is opened in the chores file here. The block is the cycle's only home until close-out
moves it. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

**Why the acceptance check:** a cycle's own checklists are per-commit instruments and every one
of them can pass while the banner claim is false. Measured in a seven-cycle program opened
against "end subprocess spawning": its close-out claimed the goal met, with about twenty spawn
sites surviving, two inside the facade the program built. A measurement or performance claim is
the shape most exposed, since "we measured it" is easy to believe and hard to notice you have not
done. Being provisional, the check can also be revised *toward* what was achieved, which is the
same failure by a slower route. A changed check is one of the things the deliberation justifies.

## Committing vs pushing

A cycle rung is committed *by* `vc-x1 push`. Never pre-commit it with `jj commit`. Push's
commit stages commit both repos with the approved title/body and stamp each new commit's
`ochid:` trailer (see [ochid trailers](jj.md#cross-repo-linking-ochid-trailers)). A
pre-committed rung leaves `@` empty and push mints a stamped empty duplicate. In
an instruction, "commit", "push", and "commit + push" all mean `vc-x1 push`. A bare `jj commit`
is asked for by name ("local commit", "just `jj commit`") and is only for work that never
publishes (local-only saves and loop-and-squash intermediates), with no `ochid:`. The approval
around a push, interactive by default and waived only by an explicit scoped delegation, is the
cycle protocol's [Pushing policy](cycle-protocol.md#policy).

## Topic bookmarks are drafts

A topic bookmark is a draft until it lands on a permanent branch. Pushed there is not published.
So keep the series inside it self-consistent: inserting or reordering a step edits the ladder in
the rungs that already committed an older version of it, not only at the tip.

- **Amend content, never re-describe.** Editing `TODO.md` in a rung and amending is not a
  `jj describe`, so hard rule 4 stays intact and the `ochid:` trailers ride along untouched
  (they carry change ids, which survive a rewrite).
- **Then force-push the bookmark**, under the same approval as any other push.
- **Exceptions, where self-consistency is not worth its cost**: the bookmark has already landed;
  another branch is stacked on it, so the rewrite becomes someone else's rebase; or the ladder
  is long and only a trailing snapshot disagrees.

The squash-form ladder below never meets this, since nothing on it is pushed. The rule is for the
multi-commit shape, whose rungs publish one at a time. Full statement in the protocol's
[Topic bookmarks are drafts](cycle-protocol.md#topic-bookmarks-are-drafts).

## Per-commit checklist

Every commit (Preparation, each Work commit, Close-out), per the protocol's
[Per-commit flow](cycle-protocol.md#per-commit-flow):

1. Mark the rung `(current)` in `TODO.md > ## In Progress`, as the first edit.
2. Do the work. On any deviation from the agreed plan, or any question, stop and surface it.
3. Flip `(current)` -> `(done)`, before validation and the commit, and write the rung's
   `Ladder details` subsection when it has conceptual content (exact title as its heading; the
   ladder itself stays a bare ToC). See the protocol's
   [Preparation](cycle-protocol.md#preparation).
4. Bump the version-of-record to this commit's version (the suffix scheme is in
   [versioning.md](versioning.md)). The opening checklist's bump already covers a Preparation
   commit.
5. Validate the artifact (the medium-specific commands are in [custom.md](../custom.md)).
   Skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out.
6. Stop and ask the user, "please review", as this is the bottom of the review loop. Do not present
   a description as we iterate until the user reviews and says "continue|go|.." indicating the work
   review is likely complete.
7. Once the work review is complete, write the description: a conventional title, then a problem
   statement and a solution statement, both broad, sized per prose.md's
   [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths). No version in either, no file list (the diff is the
   mechanical record), and no deliberation (chores, todo, and the session hold that). See
   [Commit description](cycle-protocol.md#commit-description).
8. Show title + body and stop for review. This review covers the push only when the user's go
   explicitly includes it.
9. On the user's go: `vc-x1 push <bookmark> --title "..." --body "..."`. Never pre-commit with
   `jj commit`; never hand-write `ochid:` trailers.

## Ladder (sub-cycle) checklist

Within a sub-cycle ladder, per the protocol's
[per-Work-commit contract](cycle-protocol.md#per-work-commit-contract-within-a-ladder):

1. `jj new -R .`: fresh empty `@`.
2. Do the commit's work.
3. Run the fast validation (named in [custom.md](../custom.md)). Non-negotiable.
4. `jj describe -m "..." -m "..." -R .`: scratch working title. This first-time authoring is
   the one permitted describe. The commit is never published and never carries a trailer.

Nothing on a ladder is pushed. The close-out squash
(`jj squash --from "<base>..@-" --into @ -u -R .`) collapses it, and `vc-x1 push` then
publishes the single commit.

## Before any push

- This specific push has the user's explicit approval. Approval of a plan that includes a push
  is not push approval. "Commit and push" names the destination, not a waiver of the reviews.
  Only an explicit scoped delegation ("do all of X, don't check in") waives the stops, for that
  bounded task only. Destructive ops still pause.
- Validation ran, and passed, after the last edit.
- Closing words are already written. Nothing follows the turn's final push (next checklist).

## After the final push: hard stop

Once the turn's final push or bot-repo squash-push is invoked, do no further work: no
verification, no summary, no next-step offers, no edits, until the user speaks. Put all closing
words *before* the invoke. The harness rejects an empty turn, so it may force a visible token
after the tool returns. If so, emit a bare acknowledgment only (e.g. "landed"), never a summary
or more work. Post-push verification happens next turn at the user's direction. A standing
delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps; the hard stop lands on the turn's *final*
push. See
[After push or squash-push](cycle-protocol.md#after-push-or-squash-push-stop-and-wait).

## Close-out checklist

The cycle's last step, per the protocol's
[Close-out](cycle-protocol.md#close-out):

1. **Run the acceptance check** the opening stated, and record what it showed in the
   `## In Progress` block, whether or not it passed. A check that was never run is a failed
   close-out, and a check that failed is a finding, not a reason to quietly restate the banner.
2. **Finalize the six items in place**: sync the title if the scope shifted, replace the
   provisional solution statement with what was done, drop the ladder's `(current)` / `(done)`
   markers, add any design subsections.
3. **Move the block** into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, which is what creates the section.
   Four transforms, two of which fail silently: headings one level deeper, rung refs renumbered
   into the destination's namespace, repo-root-relative links gain `../`, forward-looking notes
   rewritten. See [Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). Add the title-only
   `## Table of Contents` entry.
4. Write the `## Done` entry: the version, then a bold title line with its chores `[N]` ref,
   detail as sub-bullets (see [Done entry form](notes.md#done-entry-form)). Replace the
   `## In Progress` block with `_No cycle currently in progress._`.
5. Full validation, mandatory.
6. Update `notes/README.md` if functionality changed.
7. At push time, surface the shape options (squash / trapezoid / keep separate) and wait for
   the user's choice. The trapezoid recipe is
   [in the protocol](cycle-protocol.md#trapezoid-close-out-recipe). Its step 4 is
   `jj git push`, not `vc-x1 push`.
8. **Land the bookmark** on the user's go. Until this, nothing the cycle pushed is permanent. See
   [Cycle bookmarks](jj.md#cycle-bookmarks-create-and-land).
9. Backfill the chores as-built ladder refs (and any remaining legacy `Commits:` lines) for the
   commits landing just made permanent, which is the whole cycle rather than the previous push's
   share. Never record a SHA that is not on a permanent branch. The backfill edits ride the next
   push (a commit cannot record its own SHA).

## vc-x1 push behaviors to keep in mind

Three, independent of project language:

- **No checks of the project's own.** vc-x1 assumes nothing about a repo's contents beyond
  `.jj` and `.vc-config.toml`, and runs no build or tests. The medium's validation is the
  per-commit flow's job, run *before* invoking `vc-x1 push`. The one check that remains is
  `push-work` verifying the bookmark's remote refs are tracked, which is its own precondition.
- **Rerunning is safe.** Push keeps no state and cannot resume. Every stage no-ops when its
  work is already done, so a failed run is re-run, not resumed. If a run fails, push stops and
  reports. Getting the repos back to a sensible state is the user's call, not something the
  tool infers.
- **ochid trailers** are injected by `vc-x1 push` itself, so don't hand-write them into the
  commit body or `--title`/`--body`.

message.content: I asked how does generate and regenerate differ, if we have one source of truth, vc-config.toml, then I'd assume we'd also just generate from that? Thoughts only.

content.text:
Thoughts only, and the question is sharper than it first looks, because it exposes what these files actually are.

If `.vc-config.toml` were pure generator output, you'd be right: there'd be no "re" — every build of the file would just be *generate*, the way `init` does for a brand-new workspace, and committing generator output at all would be questionable (you'd derive it on demand).

But the committed file isn't pure output. It's two species of content interleaved:

1. **Live state the prototype cannot know**: the `[repos]` table's actual values (this checkout's paths — environment, not schema) and any *active* uncommented keys the user has set. The generator can render role-shaped defaults for these, but it can't know what a particular workspace has chosen.
2. **Generated commentary**: the schema doc-blocks, which are pure derivation from `vc-config.toml` and are the part that rotted (the fossil `[push]` block).

So the honest operation on an *existing* workspace is: re-derive part 2 and lay it back into a file whose part 1 must survive. That's what "regenerate" is naming — and it's exactly the operation the next rung turns into a tool, `config --refresh` ("rewrites a file's commented schema block while preserving active keys and `[repos]`"), with `--check` making the drift loud.

This rung gets to cheat: as far as I've seen, both sides' live parts coincide with the canned role renders (no active keys, `[repos]` matching `DualWork`/`DualBot` defaults), so a full overwrite happens to preserve everything — a hand regenerate that degenerates into a generate. That coincidence is also why the by-hand approach is safe *here* but not in general, which is the whole case for `--refresh` existing.

The plain version: with one source of truth you do just generate — but only the commentary is generated. The file also holds this workspace's own settings, which generation must not clobber, and "regenerate" is the word for "redo the generated part, keep the rest." This rung can overwrite wholesale only because this workspace happens to have nothing custom set.

(Status note: before your interrupt I'd flipped the rung to `(current)` in TODO.md — no other edits made.)

message.content: Are you saying vc-config.toml defines what are the fields in .vc-config.toml but the values currently in .vc-config.toml are to be retained? Thoughts only, I may have this totally confused.

content.text:
Yes — that's the model, with one refinement about which "values" live where.

`vc-config.toml` (repo root, unhidden, one copy) is the **schema prototype**: it defines what settable keys exist, and for each one its documentation, its type, who consumes it, its **default value**, and its reference link. build.rs bakes that into the binary. So defaults are values too, and they come from the prototype.

`.vc-config.toml` (hidden, one per side) is the **instance**: what this particular workspace has chosen. It holds two kinds of content:

- **Chosen values** — the `[repos]` paths, and any key the user has uncommented and set. These are this workspace's facts, not derivable from the prototype. These are what's retained.
- **The commented block** — pure rendering of the prototype: each key's doc lines plus a commented-out `# key = <default>` line showing what you'd get if you did nothing. These lines *look* like values, but they're documentation of the defaults, and they're exactly the part that gets thrown away and re-rendered.

The fossil `[push]` block in the current files is the second kind gone stale: commentary describing keys the binary no longer has. Nobody ever *set* `state-dir`; the file was just still displaying an old binary's documentation.

A familiar shape: it's like software that ships an `nginx.conf.default` documenting every option, while you maintain your own `nginx.conf`. The prototype is the shipped reference; the instance is your file; regenerating is updating your file's inline documentation to the new reference without touching the settings you actually made.

The plain version: yes — `vc-config.toml` says what fields exist and what their defaults are; `.vc-config.toml`'s actively-set values (here, just `[repos]`) are kept; everything commented in it is disposable rendering that this rung rebuilds from the prototype.

message.content: What about a "convert" sub-command that takes the current relatively simple .vc-config.toml and converts it to the new vc-config.toml form and the users then have only one source of truth, vc-config.toml?

content.text:
Thoughts only — and I want to first pull apart two files that the word "convert" would merge, because I think the proposal makes the rot problem worse rather than better, though it points at a real alternative worth naming.

**The two files hold truths about different things.** The prototype `vc-config.toml` is source code of the *vc-x1 product*: it defines what keys exist, their types, docs, defaults. It exists in one place (this repo), gets compiled into the binary, and every workspace running that binary inherits it. A workspace's `.vc-config.toml` holds truth about *that workspace*: its repo paths, its chosen overrides. Those aren't two sources for one truth; they're one source each for two truths. No format change can merge them, because the schema truth ships inside the binary to workspaces that will never see this repo.

**What convert would actually do**: rewriting a workspace's instance into the rich per-key-table form means copying the schema metadata (docs, defaults, references) into every workspace as *structured data*. Today that metadata appears in instances only as comments — acknowledged disposable rendering, rebuildable by `--refresh`. Promoted to real TOML tables, it becomes state the workspace owns: when the binary's schema moves, every workspace's embedded metadata is now wrong in a load-bearing place, not a cosmetic one. The fossil `[push]` block was annoying; a fossil `default =` field that tooling might *read* is a bug. So convert would take the disease this cycle is curing — derived content rotting inside instance files — and multiply it across every key.

**But the impulse — "stop having two forms" — has a legitimate radical version**, in the opposite direction: make the instance file carry *no* derived content at all. Strip `.vc-config.toml` to just `[repos]` plus actively-set keys (for this workspace, six lines), and let `vc-x1 config` — which already prints the full documented schema from the binary — be the only documentation surface. Then nothing committed can rot, and `--refresh`/`--check` become unnecessary rather than necessary. The cost: opening the file cold no longer shows you what's settable; you have to know to run `vc-x1 config`. The current design pays the rot risk (mitigated by `--check`) to keep the file self-documenting. That's a real trade, and it's the version of your idea I'd take seriously if the self-documenting property turns out not to earn its upkeep.

The plain version: the two files can't become one source of truth because they answer different questions — "what can be set" (shipped with the binary) versus "what did this workspace set." Converting instances to the rich form would copy the binary's answer into every workspace, where it goes stale — more rot, not less. The genuinely single-source move would be the opposite: shrink the instance to only what the workspace set, and let the binary do all the documenting. Worth weighing, but it's a different cycle than this rung.

content.text:
Thoughts only still — and I think the delete-the-old-file framing surfaces the crux, because it shows the proposal is solving a file-count problem that a member workspace doesn't actually have.

**From a workspace's seat, there is already only one file.** The prototype `vc-config.toml` exists solely in the vc-x1 repo, as source code — a member repo like iiac-perf's has never seen it and never will; it just runs a binary that has the schema baked in. Each workspace side today carries exactly one config file, `.vc-config.toml`. So the conversion wouldn't take users from two files to one; it would change the *format* (and name) of the one file they already have. The "two sources" feeling comes from this repo being special — it's both a workspace (has instances) and the product's home (has the prototype). Every other member only has the first role.

**And the format change doesn't buy single-truth, because the mix is intrinsic.** After conversion, the surviving rich-form file would hold `value =` entries (workspace's truth) alongside `doc` / `default` / `reference` fields (the binary's truth, copied in). That's the same authoritative-plus-cached mix the current file has — except today the cached part is *comments*, which the format itself declares non-authoritative and no parser will ever trust. Promoted to real TOML fields, a stale `default = ".vc-x1"` sits there looking machine-readable, and sooner or later something reads it. Both designs need a refresh mechanism when the binary's schema moves; the comment form fails cosmetic when stale, the data form fails load-bearing. Deleting the old file changes none of this — the objection was never about coexistence, only about what the surviving file contains.

**If the itch is "the workspace file should contain no copied truth at all"**, that's the minimal-instance direction from my last message — shrink the file to `[repos]` plus set keys, document via `vc-x1 config` — and it gets to genuine single-source by *removing* the cached half rather than restructuring it.

One more practical note: the conversion would ripple through everything that reads or writes the instance — the config reader, `--validate`, `init`, the family's existing repos, and the two `--refresh` rungs already laddered — so if it were adopted it'd be its own cycle, with this rung's regenerate likely mooted rather than amended.

The plain version: members already have just one config file; the prototype is vc-x1's internal source code, not a second user file. Converting the workspace file to the prototype's shape wouldn't unify truth — it would re-house the binary's documentation as data that can go stale dangerously instead of comments that go stale harmlessly. If we want fewer copies of truth, the move is stripping the workspace file down, not enriching it.

content.text:
Thoughts only — now I understand the shape: members carry the rich format, the binary reads their values from it, and only vc-x1's own copy feeds codegen. That's coherent, and it does have one real attraction (one format everywhere, one parser, one mental model). But walking through what a member's file would actually be, I think the comment form is doing quiet work the rich form loses.

**The information content is identical either way.** After this rung regenerates, a member's `.vc-config.toml` shows every key's doc, used-by, default, and reference — the same metadata the rich form would carry, just packaged as comments instead of TOML tables. Members already use their file as pure source of values; nothing about the current design has them generating anything. So the proposal changes packaging, not capability.

**What the comment packaging buys is ownership clarity.** In today's file there is one crisp act that marks a value as *the workspace's choice*: uncommenting the line. Everything commented is visibly the binary's voice; everything active is the user's. The rich form erases that boundary. A member's file would say `default = 68` inside a key's table — and a user who wants col-width 80 will naturally edit that field, because it's the field with a number in it. Now `--refresh` cannot tell cache from choice: is `default = ".vc-x1"` a fossil to replace or a setting to preserve? You can engineer around it — decree that only a `value =` field is ever the user's and refresh clobbers all else unconditionally — but that rule has to be taught and remembered, where "uncommented means mine" enforces itself. There's also the quieter hazard that stale metadata *as data* is machine-readable: some future tool parses the file and trusts a cached default the binary no longer has. Stale comments can mislead a human; stale fields can mislead programs.

**And the member file can't actually be the prototype's format anyway.** It needs `[repos]` with real per-checkout paths, which the prototype doesn't have, and it doesn't need `kind`/`required`/rendering-order semantics, which the prototype does. So we'd end up with two dialects of the rich form — the uniformity that motivates the idea thins out on contact.

One separable piece worth keeping: if part of the appeal is the *name* — visible `vc-config.toml` rather than hidden `.vc-config.toml` — that rename stands on its own and could be done without any format change, same species of move as `.claude` to `.agent-session`.

The plain version: members would get the same documentation either way; the question is whether the binary's half of the file is comments or data. Comments make "which lines are mine" self-evident and make staleness harmless; data makes both ambiguous, which is exactly where refresh tooling gets fragile. I'd keep the instance format as-is, and treat "unhide the filename" as the piece of this worth considering on its own.

content.text:
Thoughts only — and this is a genuine reframe: you're proposing the schema files join the *pinned family file* mechanism. Official copies in the payload, every member carries its own, a member's edits are its proposal set, convergence folds them back. That answers my rot objection with the family's existing machinery — drift stops being decay and becomes a diff with a review path. It's the strongest version of the idea so far. Two things still push back, and one consequence falls out that I think settles the earlier thread.

**First: pinning and value-carrying are mutually exclusive.** The diff-against-payload mechanism works because a pinned file's diff *means something*: every divergence is a proposal. If members also set their working values in their `vc-config.toml` copy, the diff fills with per-workspace preferences that are explicitly *not* proposals — iiac-perf's col-width choice isn't a suggestion that the family change the default. You'd have to eyeball which diff hunks are proposals and which are settings, and the property that made the mechanism attractive (the diff needs no maintenance and cannot lie) is gone. So if these files are pinned, values must stay somewhere else — which is `.vc-config.toml` doing exactly its current job. Your proposal, taken to its conclusion, *requires* the instance file to survive rather than replacing it.

**Second: unlike agent-files, these files describe a binary, and a copy can disagree with the binary the member runs.** Agent-files can't skew this way — the copy *is* the behavior, self-contained. But a member's `vc-config.toml` copy has no local consumer: build.rs only runs in vc-x1's repo, so editing the copy changes nothing about the tool the member invokes. That's fine for its role as a proposal surface, but it invites a silent failure — someone edits a default in the prototype copy expecting behavior to change, and nothing happens. And between syncs, the copy documents a schema the member's installed binary may not have.

That second objection lands differently on the two files, which suggests splitting them:

- **`vc-config.md` distributes well.** It's long-form documentation humans actually read, the same species as `agent-data/*`. With `reference-base` repointed at the member's own repo (your init idea), every generated `reference:` line in the member's instance file resolves to the copy the member carries — local, offline, and annotatable in place as a proposal. And the laddered `validate-anchors` rung would then have real work in member repos: checking that the carried copy still anchors what the instance links to.
- **The prototype `vc-config.toml` distributes poorly.** It's build input, meaningful only where the build runs. A member's proposal about a default or a doc one-liner could ride as a diff on it, but the same proposal is expressible against `vc-config.md`, which the member has a reason to carry anyway. Carrying inert build-source invites the edit-and-nothing-happens trap for no gain the md file doesn't already provide.

On the mechanics you sketched: init already knows the template payload, so seeding copies and stamping `reference-base` with the target's own URL is a natural fit — though note `reference-base` currently lives in the *instance* file's `[vc-config]` section, so init writing it per-repo is exactly the existing pattern.

The plain version: making the schema files pinned family files is the version of this idea that works — rot becomes reviewable drift. But it forces a clean division of labor: pinned copies carry *proposals and docs*, the instance `.vc-config.toml` carries *this workspace's values*, and they can't merge without wrecking the diff-as-proposal property. I'd distribute `vc-config.md` (with locally-resolving references), keep the prototype TOML as vc-x1 build source only, and leave the instance file as it is.

content.text:
Thoughts only — yes, that's the shape, with two corrections at the edges where the mechanism would otherwise mislead.

**Correction one: the comment blocks in `.vc-config.toml` are not an editable doc surface.** That text is generator output — rendered from the schema baked into the binary, and rewritten wholesale by the coming `config --refresh`. A member who improves the wording there loses the edit at the next refresh, and nothing diffs it against anything, because the instance file is per-workspace values, not a pinned file with a payload counterpart. So the division stays crisp: in `.vc-config.toml` you edit exactly one thing — values (uncomment, set). Doc improvements go in the `vc-config.md` copy, the pinned file whose diff *is* the proposal. If someone's doc fix targets a key's one-liner — which lives in the prototype, not the md — their md edit can still carry it in prose, and convergence moves it into the prototype where it belongs.

**Correction two: "try a new field" splits into two different acts.** Today `config --validate` rejects unknown keys, so a member can't invent a field locally even for private use — that's the exact pain already on record in `custom-family.md` (member name and template path belong in config but can't move there yet), tracked by the `[private]` table proposal. Once that lands, a workspace that wants extra fields *for itself* puts them under `[private]`, no fork needed. Proposing a new field *for the schema* — one the binary should validate, document, and default — necessarily means changing the prototype and rebuilding, so it's a vc-x1 change: family members route it through the family's own channel (mailbox, or a diff discussed at convergence — vc-x1 is just another member whose repo is where schema edits physically land), while an outside adopter forks and proposes back, as you say.

So the full picture, per member:

- `.vc-config.toml` — this workspace's values, the only behavior-changing file; its comments are disposable rendering.
- `vc-config.md` — pinned copy, locally-resolving references, and the doc-proposal surface via its diff.
- `[private]` (once it exists) — workspace-local extras without schema blessing.
- Prototype `vc-config.toml` — lives in vc-x1 only; schema proposals travel to it by family channel or fork.

The plain version: agreed, with two guardrails — the instance file's comments are machine-owned and never worth editing, and new fields come in two flavors: private ones will get a sanctioned `[private]` home so no fork is needed, while real schema additions are by nature vc-x1 changes and travel as proposals to it.

content.text:
Thoughts only — yes, and I think with that the pieces click together rather than conflict.

The `reference:` line in every generated key block is exactly that link, and it's already built to be repointable: the URL is derived at render time from `[vc-config] reference-base` + `/blob/HEAD/` + the key's heading anchor in `vc-config.md`. Nothing about the target is baked in. So with your init idea — new member's `reference-base` stamped to its own repo, `vc-config.md` seeded from the payload — every comment block in a member's `.vc-config.toml` links to *the copy that member owns and may edit*. The two roles stop competing and compose:

- The **comments** stay machine-owned rendering: always regenerable, never worth editing, guaranteed current by `--refresh --check`.
- The **link target** is the human-owned surface: the member's pinned `vc-config.md`, where an edit is legitimate, survives every refresh, and is automatically a proposal because the file diffs against the payload.

So a member who reads a key's comment and finds the docs wanting follows the reference, edits their own `vc-config.md`, and the family mechanism carries the improvement from there. No one needs to touch generated text, and nothing they write gets clobbered.

Two existing guards already serve this: the prototype rung's drift test requires every derived reference to anchor at a real `vc-config.md` heading (a key without docs fails the build), and the laddered `validate-anchors` extends that species of check into member repos, where it can verify the carried copy still has the headings the instance links to.

The plain version: agreed — the comments don't need to be editable because they link to the file that is. Machine text links to human text; refresh keeps the first current, the pinned-file diff makes edits to the second into proposals. That was the missing piece that makes the whole distribution story coherent.

content.text:
Thoughts only — agreed, and the useful move is noticing the design already embraces it, at two different altitudes with two different durabilities.

The durable edit point is `reference-base` itself: it's a settable key in the instance file, an *active* value, so it survives every refresh and repoints all the links at once. A member who wants references landing on their fork, an internal mirror, or anywhere else sets one line and the whole rendered surface follows. That's link-editing as a first-class, embraced act — the tooling was built around it.

Editing an individual rendered line is also genuinely theirs to do — it's their file, TOML ignores comments, `--validate` won't blink, and nothing runs behind their back to undo it. The honest framing is that such an edit is *ephemeral by contract* rather than forbidden: `config --refresh` is a tool the member invokes, not a daemon, so a hand-tuned comment persists exactly as long as they choose not to refresh. And `--refresh --check` gives them the polite version of the deal — it reports that their file diverges from what the binary would render, without touching anything. The member who values their hand edits over the currency guarantee just reads `--check`'s output and declines the rewrite. That *is* embracing it: the tool informs, the human decides, nothing is enforced.

If a real pattern emerged — say members wanting one specific key's link aimed somewhere special while the rest follow `reference-base` — the prototype already has a per-key reference-override notion vc-x1-side, and an instance-side counterpart would be the schema-blessed way to make that particular edit durable. I'd wait for the itch before building it, but it's the natural extension if "embrace" needs more room.

The plain version: they can edit anything, and the design says yes at both levels — `reference-base` is the edit that lasts and moves all links together, while hand-edits to rendered comments are honored by simply never refreshing uninvited, with `--check` showing the drift instead of erasing it. Freedom stays with the file's owner; the tool only offers currency, never imposes it.
