content.content:
1	# Notes file conventions
2	
3	Conventions the bot follows when reading and writing notes files (`TODO.md`,
4	`notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`, `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, `notes/done.md`). One
5	source of truth lives here, and [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this
6	before editing a notes file.
7	
8	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
9	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
10	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
11	
12	## File reads: read the slice you need
13	
14	Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs. Grep or read
15	further on demand.
16	
17	- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In
18	  Progress` + the top of the ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
19	  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`. Read further only when chasing a
20	  lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
21	- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`**: the long-tail backlog (lower-priority entries below the ranked
22	  `## Todo`). Read only when picking up a backlog item, and grep to locate it first.
23	- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small, so read it whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
24	  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
25	- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
26	  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
27	  need.
28	
29	**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
30	bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline. The same "slice you need" rule applies
31	to historical files.
32	
33	## Notes references
34	
35	Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
36	for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
37	`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay
38	single-bracketed.
39	
40	## Reference numbering
41	
42	Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
43	file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
44	`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
45	completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.
46	
47	Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
48	`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
49	file's number. To cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
50	define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code
51	span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key
52	(often from another file's namespace), data, not a citation, so it needs no definition here. To
53	point at a section of another file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor,
54	`[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a bare number.
55	
56	A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or
57	`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
58	`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a rung of a section's
59	as-built ladder. See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the
60	exact shape.
61	
62	A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
63	first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md`: `## Todo`
64	then `## Done`; `chores-NN.md`: top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
65	appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
66	definitions move. Every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
67	span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
68	namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule: `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
69	land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate; `chores-NN.md` / `done.md` are
70	append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
71	slots out of document order).
72	
73	## Markdown anchor links
74	
75	GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
76	spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
77	(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
78	markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
79	official spec for auto-generated anchors. The de-facto reference implementation is
80	[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).
81	
82	## Todo format
83	
84	`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest;
85	long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
86	(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
87	description with reference links to more detail.
88	
89	`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
90	`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending); for `## Bugs` it's just
91	an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
92	reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
93	normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
94	durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
95	renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.
96	
97	Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
98	an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
99	fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
100	wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
101	title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.
102	
103	`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews, and `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
104	`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.
105	
106	Example shape:
107	
108	```
109	# Todo
110	1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
111	2. Fix bug Y [[1]]
112	
113	# Done
114	- **Fixed issue Z** [[2]],[[3]]
115	
116	[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
117	[2]: issues.md#issue-z
118	[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
119	```
120	
121	## Done entry form
122	
123	A `## Done` entry (in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`) is the close-out's **version**, then a **bold
124	title line** carrying its chores `[[N]]` ref, with any detail as sub-bullets:
125	
126	```
127	- 0.42.0 **feat: config loader** [[7]]
128	  - `--config` resolves per-profile pin pools
129	  - the parse rejects unknown keys rather than ignoring them
130	```
131	
132	- **Bold, and detail below rather than beside.** These entries are read by skimming a list for
133	  one of them, so the title has to be findable without reading the line it sits on. A title
134	  followed by a paragraph of summary is the wall-of-prose shape
135	  [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) warns about, and it hides the one thing a skim is looking
136	  for. Bold matches the `## In Progress` block, whose title line is already bold.
137	- **The version leads and the title stays bold**, so the entry answers both questions a reader
138	  brings: `grep 0.42.0` finds what shipped in a version, and the eye still lands on titles when
139	  skimming. Putting the version *inside* the bold, or dropping the bold for a plain rung-shaped
140	  line, trades one of those for the other. See
141	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
142	  for why a Done entry may carry a version at all when a ladder rung may not.
143	- **A one-liner is still fine** when the title says it all. The sub-bullets are for when it does
144	  not. What is not fine is the middle case, a title with sentences trailing off it.
145	- **Sub-bullets are conceptual, like chores bullets**: what shipped, not a file list, and never
146	  a copy of the chores intro. The `[[N]]` ref is what carries a reader to the full narrative.
147	- **Entries written before this convention keep their form** and gain a version when touched. A
148	  sweep would rewrite history's presentation for no reader's benefit.
149	
150	## Retiring Done entries
151	
152	`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
153	log. Move entries into `done.md` at these natural beats:
154	
155	- **Closing a ladder**: when the close-out commit ships, decide which prior entries are no
156	  longer needed for nearby context and migrate them. The entry form is the same in both files
157	  (see [Done entry form](#done-entry-form)), so a migration moves the bullet as it stands.
158	- **Opening a new ladder**: at the opening step, do the same sweep before bumping the
159	  version-of-record.
160	- **Resolving an agent-file experiment**: at the beat where it resolves, not at a ladder
161	  boundary. Adopted and rejected retire identically, since "we tried this and dropped it" is what
162	  history serves worst. The narrative goes in a `chores-NN.md` section and the dogfood entry is
163	  removed from wherever the project keeps its log, so that log carries in-flight entries only. See
164	  [Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files).
165	
166	Migration mechanics:
167	
168	- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
169	  number).
170	- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
171	  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
172	- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
173	  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.
174	
175	## Chores conventions
176	
177	### Headings and entries that record a commit
178	
179	A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records. See
180	[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
181	rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
182	`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. **No title carries a
183	version.** The two records that carry one carry it beside the title, never inside it, and both
184	are records of a commit (the backfilled as-built rung and the `## Done` entry). See
185	[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
186	E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
187	`- 0.42.0 **refactor: extract config loader** [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out
188	commit's title, and its shape is in [Done entry form](#done-entry-form).
189	
190	This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
191	`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section. Those are named for
192	whatever fits. A `Ladder details` rung subsection is the exception among subsections: it is
193	commit-recording, its heading the rung's exact title. Among the commit-recording ones, exact
194	match is the strong default (nothing absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a
195	record up with its commit.
196	
197	A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress. The *last* edit before
198	`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
199	commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm. The
200	pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
201	too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).
202	
203	Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
204	free-form text. The convention applies going forward.
205	
206	### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record
207	
208	A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header, below), then
209	[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) (intro + bullets) for what landed and why, and any `###`
210	design subsections, the moved block's `Ladder details` area among them (its subsections are
211	rung-titled and commit-recording, unlike the free-named design ones). Bullets here are
212	**conceptual** (design points, structural notes), never a per-file edit list. Nothing in prose keeps one: the **diff** is the source of truth for what
213	changed mechanically (`git show --stat`, immutable, naturally scoped to the commit), the **commit
214	body** states the problem and the solution in broad terms, and the **chores section** is the
215	source of truth for the design thinking. Each of the three cross-links to the others; none
216	restates another.
217	
218	The section is **not built up here**: it is created at close-out by moving the cycle's
219	`## In Progress` block, which was its single home while the cycle ran. So a rung is appended, and
220	narrative written, in `TODO.md` as each step lands, and close-out moves the finished block rather
221	than assembling a second copy of it. Full when-in-the-cycle timing lives in cycle-protocol.md
222	[Chores sections](cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections). This note is the pointer, so the
223	two don't drift.
224	
225	**Why one home:** the alternative keeps a working ladder in `TODO.md` and an as-built ladder in
226	chores, so every rung is written twice and every backfill applied twice. Detail written twice
227	drifts, which is the same argument that keeps the edit list out of the commit body.
228	
229	When the intro starts wanting to explain a mechanism, hypothesis, or wrinkle, don't inflate it.
230	Promote that to its own `###` subsection inside the same `chores-NN.md`. If the wrinkle is a
231	live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a
232	`TODO.md` item with a `[N]` ref pointing at that subsection (todo->chores is the normal ref
233	direction).
234	
235	**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
236	places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; the body owns the problem
237	and the solution; chores owns the narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.
238	
239	### Chores commit references
240	
241	The first content under a chores section header is the **as-built ladder**: one rung per
242	commit the section records, in landing order, each rung carrying its own `[N]` citation slot.
243	The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit. A single-commit cycle is a
244	one-rung ladder whose one step is the close-out:
245	
246	```
247	## refactor: extract config loader
248	
249	- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 refactor: split loader from parser
250	- [[N]] refactor: extract config loader
251	
252	<intro paragraph...>
253	```
254	
255	- The rung form is `- [[N]] <title>` while the commit is unlanded, becoming
256	  `- [[2]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>` at backfill, as the first rung above shows. No step number and no
257	  `(current)` / `(done)` marker, since as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in
258	  `TODO.md > ## In Progress`). Landing order is the list order. See
259	  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
260	- **The version arrives with the SHA, not before it.** It is the one version written into prose
261	  (see
262	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
263	  because here it records what a landed commit carried rather than naming a step, and together
264	  with the SHA it decodes an old `-V` banner. On an unlanded branch it is as rewritable as the
265	  SHA, so it waits for the same moment (Timing, below). The version is knowable earlier, from the
266	  manifest. Holding it back is deliberate, buying one timing rule and a record a rebase cannot
267	  falsify.
268	- Two headers in one chores file must not share a title, or their anchors collide and the
269	  duplicate silently resolves to the first. Within a file that is the whole uniqueness
270	  requirement. Titles may repeat across the repo's history.
271	- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real
272	  file-local slot once its commit's SHA is permanent (see Timing below).
273	- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
274	  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
275	  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`
276	  resolves against its `[3]:` definition, and CommonMark / GitHub / VS Code all do this.) The
277	  `# References` definition puts the **commit URL** as the destination, with the **full
278	  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:
279	
280	```
281	[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
282	```
283	
284	- The 12-hex short SHA in the URL keeps it short, and GitHub / GitLab resolve a unique prefix to
285	  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).
286	- The full SHA in the title is host-agnostic and unambiguous: it survives a repo host change,
287	  `git show <40-hex>` works in any clone, and external tooling scraping the notes (a database,
288	  say) gets the canonical identifier.
289	
290	**Timing.** A commit's SHA isn't stable until it lands on a **permanent branch** (`main`, or a
291	long-lived release/patch branch), because a rebase or squash rewrites it on the way, and neither
292	is its version. A commit can't record its own SHA, so the fill lands one push later: every rung
293	opens with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and no version, and each push backfills the rungs of
294	the commits the previous push made permanent. On a topic branch a section waits until the branch
295	lands. The commit itself is the record, and `git log --grep "<title>"` finds it. See
296	cycle-protocol [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill).
297	
298	Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines. The ladder form applies
299	going forward.
300	
301	### Chores file Table of Contents
302	
303	Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
304	first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
305	section, in file order.
306	
307	- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
308	  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
309	- The entry is appended by the close-out move that creates the section, and the entry text
310	  participates in the same last-edit title sync as the section header and the `## Done` entry.
311	- Design `###` subsections stay out of the TOC.
312	- Files predating the convention gain a TOC opportunistically, not on a schedule.

# Notes file conventions

Conventions the bot follows when reading and writing notes files (`TODO.md`,
`notes/todo-backlog.md`, `notes/bugs.md`, `notes/chores/chores-NN.md`, `notes/done.md`). One
source of truth lives here, and [`notes/README.md`](../notes/README.md) points back. Read this
before editing a notes file.

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## File reads: read the slice you need

Long notes files are appended to over time. Read only the slice your task needs. Grep or read
further on demand.

- **`TODO.md`** (the routine acquaint read): the first ~60 lines covers intro + `## In
  Progress` + the top of the ranked `## Todo` (priorities, #1 highest). `Read` with
  `offset=0, limit=60`. `## Ideas` sits below `## Todo`. Read further only when chasing a
  lower-ranked entry, an Idea, a `[N]` ref, or auditing the whole list.
- **`notes/todo-backlog.md`**: the long-tail backlog (lower-priority entries below the ranked
  `## Todo`). Read only when picking up a backlog item, and grep to locate it first.
- **`notes/bugs.md`**: the bug list. Small, so read it whole when triaging a bug or chasing the
  `## Bugs` pointer in TODO.md.
- **`notes/done.md`** + **`notes/chores/chores-NN.md`**: historical / append-mostly. Scan
  headings first (`grep '^## ' notes/chores/chores-NN.md`), then read only the section you
  need.

**Why:** the routine read should stay small. `TODO.md` grows every cycle, so the backlog and
bugs live in files under `notes/` rather than inline. The same "slice you need" rule applies
to historical files.

## Notes references

Reference *citations* are double-bracketed so the brackets render: `[[N]]`, or `[[2]],[[3]]`
for several (comma-separated, not `[2,3]` or `[[2]][[3]]`). The `[N]:` definitions in a file's
`# References` section and inline `[text](url)` / `[text](#anchor)` links stay
single-bracketed.

## Reference numbering

Every note file (`TODO.md`, `todo-backlog.md`, `bugs.md`, `chores-NN.md`, `done.md`) keeps a
file-local `# References` section at the bottom. Reference numbers are scoped to that file:
`[1]` in `chores-07.md` and `[1]` in `chores-01.md` are independent slots that may point at
completely different URLs. New chores files start their numbering at `[1]`.

Treat `[N]` like a **footnote**: the number is a local slot, only meaningful within its file's
`# References`. So a `[N]` *citation* (bare `[N]`, or doubled `[[N]]`) never reuses another
file's number. To cite a target a sibling file references, pick your own next-local slot and
define it (the same target may carry a different number in each file). A `[N]` *inside a code
span* (`` `[72]` ``) is different: that's a quoted identifier, literal text naming a ref-key
(often from another file's namespace), data, not a citation, so it needs no definition here. To
point at a section of another file from prose, use an inline link with an anchor,
`[that section](../chores-07.md#...)`, not a bare number.

A `chores-NN.md` `# References` entry is usually a `/notes/<file>.md#anchor` (or
`/ARCHITECTURE.md`) path, but may also be a **commit reference**,
`[N]: <commit-url-with-12-hex-SHA> "<full-40-hex-SHA>"`, cited by a rung of a section's
as-built ladder. See [Chores commit references](#chores-commit-references) for the why and the
exact shape.

A file's `# References` can be **re-packed** to a contiguous `[1]..[N]` in
first-citation-appearance order: walk the file's prose in document order (`TODO.md`: `## Todo`
then `## Done`; `chores-NN.md`: top to bottom) and number refs as their first `[[N]]` citation
appears. This is a file-local rewrite, so only that file's `[[N]]` citations and `[N]:`
definitions move. Every target and sibling file is untouched. A `[[N]]` inside a `` ` `` code
span is a literal token, not a citation, and is left alone. Do it opportunistically (when the
namespace has drifted enough to annoy), not on a schedule: `TODO.md` fragments fastest (entries
land and get pruned every cycle) and is the usual candidate; `chores-NN.md` / `done.md` are
append-mostly and only need it after an unusual event (e.g. a bulk retrofit that allocated
slots out of document order).

## Markdown anchor links

GitHub anchor algorithm: lowercase, strip non-alphanumeric characters in place, map remaining
spaces to hyphens 1-for-1. Do **not** collapse adjacent whitespace, so `a + b` -> `a--b`
(spaces on both sides of `+`), but `a: b` -> `a-b` (only trailing space on `:`). General
markdown reference: [markdownguide.org](https://www.markdownguide.org). GitHub publishes no
official spec for auto-generated anchors. The de-facto reference implementation is
[github-slugger](https://github.com/Flet/github-slugger).

## Todo format

`TODO.md` is organized into `## In Progress`, `## Todo` (strict priority rank, #1 highest;
long-tail backlog in [todo-backlog.md](../notes/todo-backlog.md)), `## Ideas`, `## Bugs`
(pointer to [bugs.md](../notes/bugs.md)), and `## Done` sections. Each item is a short
description with reference links to more detail.

`## Todo` and `## Bugs` entries carry explicit `1.` `2.` ... numbers in the source. For
`## Todo` the number is its **priority rank** (#1 highest, descending); for `## Bugs` it's just
an index. They're for grepping and at-a-glance "let's do #1", **not stable IDs**: reorder (to
reprioritize), insert, or delete freely, then `vc-x1 fix-todo --no-dry-run` renumbers and
normalizes continuation-line indent, so any given number is positional. **To refer to a Todo
durably, name it by its title, a plain, greppable text mention.** Not its number (positional,
renumbered) and not a markdown link: a numbered list item has no anchor to link to.

Numbering helps a human orient in a long list but makes links difficult and fragile, especially
an external reference pointing in, which can't be auto-fixed when the list renumbers. A robust
fix (a number-free anchor, or a number-tolerant dereference that matches the title slug and
wildcards the numeric prefix, since a GitHub slug like `5-foo` is encoded, not opaque, so the
title is recoverable) is a `validate-numbering` design question, out of scope here.

`vc-x1 fix-todo` alone only previews, and `vc-x1 validate-todo` is the read-only check. The
`## Done` section keeps `-` bullets, since items aren't referenced by number once completed.

Example shape:

```
# Todo
1. Add new feature X [details](features.md#feature-x)
2. Fix bug Y [[1]]

# Done
- **Fixed issue Z** [[2]],[[3]]

[1]: bugs.md#bug-y
[2]: issues.md#issue-z
[3]: fixes.md#fix-z
```

## Done entry form

A `## Done` entry (in `TODO.md` and in `done.md`) is the close-out's **version**, then a **bold
title line** carrying its chores `[[N]]` ref, with any detail as sub-bullets:

```
- 0.42.0 **feat: config loader** [[7]]
  - `--config` resolves per-profile pin pools
  - the parse rejects unknown keys rather than ignoring them
```

- **Bold, and detail below rather than beside.** These entries are read by skimming a list for
  one of them, so the title has to be findable without reading the line it sits on. A title
  followed by a paragraph of summary is the wall-of-prose shape
  [Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) warns about, and it hides the one thing a skim is looking
  for. Bold matches the `## In Progress` block, whose title line is already bold.
- **The version leads and the title stays bold**, so the entry answers both questions a reader
  brings: `grep 0.42.0` finds what shipped in a version, and the eye still lands on titles when
  skimming. Putting the version *inside* the bold, or dropping the bold for a plain rung-shaped
  line, trades one of those for the other. See
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)
  for why a Done entry may carry a version at all when a ladder rung may not.
- **A one-liner is still fine** when the title says it all. The sub-bullets are for when it does
  not. What is not fine is the middle case, a title with sentences trailing off it.
- **Sub-bullets are conceptual, like chores bullets**: what shipped, not a file list, and never
  a copy of the chores intro. The `[[N]]` ref is what carries a reader to the full narrative.
- **Entries written before this convention keep their form** and gain a version when touched. A
  sweep would rewrite history's presentation for no reader's benefit.

## Retiring Done entries

`TODO.md`'s `## Done` section is a rolling buffer of recently shipped work, not a permanent
log. Move entries into `done.md` at these natural beats:

- **Closing a ladder**: when the close-out commit ships, decide which prior entries are no
  longer needed for nearby context and migrate them. The entry form is the same in both files
  (see [Done entry form](#done-entry-form)), so a migration moves the bullet as it stands.
- **Opening a new ladder**: at the opening step, do the same sweep before bumping the
  version-of-record.
- **Resolving an agent-file experiment**: at the beat where it resolves, not at a ladder
  boundary. Adopted and rejected retire identically, since "we tried this and dropped it" is what
  history serves worst. The narrative goes in a `chores-NN.md` section and the dogfood entry is
  removed from wherever the project keeps its log, so that log carries in-flight entries only. See
  [Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files).

Migration mechanics:

- Move the bullet itself from `TODO.md > ## Done` to `done.md` (preserving the original ref
  number).
- Copy any references the moved entries cite into `done.md`'s `# References` section (those
  refs are file-local, so coexisting with `TODO.md`'s namespace is fine).
- Prune any references in `TODO.md > # References` no longer cited by anything in
  `## In Progress` / `## Todo` / `## Done`. This frees the numbers for future reuse.

## Chores conventions

### Headings and entries that record a commit

A commit's title is reused verbatim across its records. See
[Conventional-commit shape](prose.md#conventional-commit-shape-ladder--chores--commit) for the
rule. Beyond the chores `##` header, that same string is used for the matching
`TODO.md > ## Done` entry and any `[N]` reference to that section. **No title carries a
version.** The two records that carry one carry it beside the title, never inside it, and both
are records of a commit (the backfilled as-built rung and the `## Done` entry). See
[Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only).
E.g. the chores header `## refactor: extract config loader` and the Done line
`- 0.42.0 **refactor: extract config loader** [[3]]`. The `## Done` entry uses the close-out
commit's title, and its shape is in [Done entry form](#done-entry-form).

This does **not** apply to organizational headings (`## Todo`, `## In Progress`,
`# References`) or to design `###` subsections inside a chores section. Those are named for
whatever fits. A `Ladder details` rung subsection is the exception among subsections: it is
commit-recording, its heading the rung's exact title. Among the commit-recording ones, exact
match is the strong default (nothing absolute): a near-miss just makes it harder to line a
record up with its commit.

A commit-recording header is provisional while the work is in progress. The *last* edit before
`vc-x1 push` syncs it, and the `## Done` entry / `[N]` anchor for that commit, to the final
commit title. See [Markdown anchor links](#markdown-anchor-links) for the slug algorithm. The
pre-commit checklist catches a dangling `#anchor`, and a future `vc-x1 validate-repo` should
too (and should verify the recorded title matches the commit).

Any pre-existing sections and `## Done` entries that predate this convention keep their
free-form text. The convention applies going forward.

### Chores section content: no edit list; git is the record

A chores section is: the as-built ladder (first content under the header, below), then

live design concern (something that *should* change, not just be recorded), also add a

direction).

**Why:** a chores edit list and the commit body were specified to be the same content in two
places, and detail written twice drifts. Git owns the mechanical record; the body owns the problem
and the solution; chores owns the narrative; the ladder's commit refs link them.

The same form is used for every cycle, single- or multi-commit. A single-commit cycle is a
one-rung ladder whose one step is the close-out:

```
## refactor: extract config loader

- [[2]] 0.42.0-1 refactor: split loader from parser
- [[N]] refactor: extract config loader

<intro paragraph...>
```

- The rung form is `- [[N]] <title>` while the commit is unlanded, becoming
  `- [[2]] X.Y.Z[-n] <title>` at backfill, as the first rung above shows. No step number and no
  `(current)` / `(done)` marker, since as-built implies done (the in-flight markers live in
  `TODO.md > ## In Progress`). Landing order is the list order. See
  [Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered).
- **The version arrives with the SHA, not before it.** It is the one version written into prose
  (see
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
  because here it records what a landed commit carried rather than naming a step, and together
  with the SHA it decodes an old `-V` banner. On an unlanded branch it is as rewritable as the
  SHA, so it waits for the same moment (Timing, below). The version is knowable earlier, from the
  manifest. Holding it back is deliberate, buying one timing rule and a record a rebase cannot

  requirement. Titles may repeat across the repo's history.
- A rung is written with the literal `[[N]]` placeholder and backfilled in place with a real

- Rung citations use the file-local `[N]` reference machinery (see
  [Reference numbering](#reference-numbering)), **double-bracketed** so the brackets render.
  (`[[3]]` shows as a literal `[`, the `[3]` link, then a literal `]`; the inner `[3]`

  40-hex SHA** in the title slot:

```
[3]: https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/commit/<12-hex> "<40-hex>"
```

  the canonical commit page (GitLab's path has a `/-/` before `commit/`).

  say) gets the canonical identifier.

Sections that predate this convention keep their `Commits:` lines. The ladder form applies
going forward.

### Chores file Table of Contents

Each `chores-NN.md` carries a `## Table of Contents` section between the file intro and the
first commit-recording section: one `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` entry per commit-recording `##`
section, in file order.

- Entries are title-only, with no version and no `[N]` refs, so the TOC never needs backfill:
  the TOC navigates, the section's as-built ladder records.
- The entry is appended by the close-out move that creates the section, and the entry text

**The rung's `Ladder details` subsection in TODO.md** now opens by saying the mechanical work is still exactly what the title names — regenerate both `.vc-config.toml` files, verify acceptance items 1-2 — and that what outgrew the title is the *ownership model* the regenerate rests on. It then records six points:

1. Wrap width goes to <=100, decided before regenerating so the files are written once.
2. `.vc-config.toml` is a workspace's only behavior-changing file: active lines are the workspace's own and always preserved; comment blocks are machine-owned rendering, disposable by construction.
3. Hand edits to rendered comments are permitted but ephemeral — refresh only runs when invoked, `--check` reports rather than rewrites, and the durable link edit is `reference-base`.
4. This rung's full overwrite is safe only because this workspace has nothing custom set; the general preserve-actives operation is the `config --refresh` rung.
5. The doc-proposal surface is `vc-config.md`, reached from the comments via each key's `reference:` link; distributing it as a pinned family file with init stamping `reference-base` per member is the agreed direction, recorded as backlog #52.
6. Schema changes stay vc-x1 changes: prototype remains build source, proposals travel by family channel or fork, workspace-local keys wait on `[private]`.

**Backlog #52** ("init distributes vc-config.md; reference-base points at the member") carries the beyond-this-cycle piece: init seeding the copy, the pinned-file diff-as-proposal mechanism, why pinning and value-carrying can't mix, and the member-side work `validate-anchors` gains.

On the title itself: I kept "chore: regenerate stale config files", because the commit this rung will make still does precisely that — the discussion produced design record, not different mechanical work, and the record now lives where the conventions put it (rung subsection + backlog). If you'd rather the title carry the model shift, say so and I'll retitle before anything commits.

Please review — and if this stands, the next act is the rung's actual work: the 72-to-100 renderer change, then the regenerate.

content.text:
Thoughts only — I'd split the question into "what must happen before regenerate" and "where does the init work live", because they have different answers.

**The part that genuinely belongs before regenerate is a decision, not the rung.** The lesson that re-scoped this cycle was "don't regenerate before the generator settles," and #52 touches the generator in exactly one place: the shape of the `reference:` line. Designing the member story could plausibly change it — the obvious candidate being whether a member's links should stay derived web URLs (`reference-base` + `/blob/HEAD/` + anchor, as built) or become repo-local relative links (`vc-config.md#anchor`), which would work offline and in-editor for the copy the member carries. If that question is open, regenerating first repeats the aborted first attempt's mistake. If we settle it — and my recommendation is *keep the derived web URL*: it's one scheme for all consumers, it works from the rendered file wherever it's viewed (terminals linkify URLs, not relative paths), and the member-local copy is still one click away since the URL points at the member's own repo — then regenerate is unblocked with no new rung in front of it.

**The init implementation itself I would not put before regenerate, and I'd hesitate to put it in this cycle at all.** Three reasons:

1. It has a real unsolved design problem: at init time the member's repo URL typically doesn't exist yet — the repo is being created, the remote comes later. Stamping `reference-base` needs an answer (an init argument, a placeholder plus later fix-up, deriving from a remote once added). That's a design rung's worth of thinking on its own.
2. It's cross-repo: the official `vc-config.md` copy has to land in the template payload, and existing members need migration — acts that belong to the template repo and convergence, not to a vc-x1 cycle rung.
3. This cycle already stretched once (validate-anchors), and #52 is close to cycle-sized. The family's own pattern would make it the *next* cycle, opened with the fresh backlog entry as its seed — which is what the backlog entry is for, and why it records the ownership model's location rather than restating it.

**If you do want it in this cycle**, the placement I'd argue for is after "feat: add config --refresh", not before regenerate: once `--refresh` exists, any rendering change a later rung causes is a cheap mechanical re-render rather than another hand-copy — so ordering refresh early is what actually removes the "regenerate too soon" risk for everything downstream, init included.

The plain version: the only thing regenerate is waiting on is agreeing the link stays a web URL built from `reference-base` — I recommend yes. The init-distributes work is heavier than it looks (unknown URL at init, template-side seeding, member migration), so I'd keep it as the next cycle's seed rather than a rung here; but if it joins this ladder, it goes after `--refresh`, because refresh is what makes later re-renders free.

the same .vc-config.toml file except the 8-3 version adds a `reference: https://...`.

I think the next rung of -dev is to add the vc-config.md file. And is there some way
for that link to reference the local file rather then the file in the repo as is possible
with a markdown file? Thoughts only.

content.text:
Thoughts only — two threads: the link question has a crisp technical answer, and the "add vc-config.md" rung has a design choice hiding in it that's worth naming before it's laddered.

**The link question: no, not portably, and the reason is structural.** A markdown relative link works because markdown is hypertext — a renderer (GitHub, an editor preview) resolves `vc-config.md#anchor` against the file's own location. A TOML comment has no renderer; what makes links clickable there is *linkification* by whatever is displaying the text (GitHub's code view, a terminal, an editor), and linkifiers key on URL schemes. So:

- `https://...` linkifies nearly everywhere — that's what the derived reference gets us.
- A bare relative path (`vc-config.md#col-width`) linkifies almost nowhere; it's just prose.
- `file://` URLs require absolute paths, which are per-machine and per-clone, so they can't be committed. Dead end for the stored file.

Two softeners. First, once `reference-base` points at the member's own repo, the web URL *is* the local file — its committed version on the member's own default branch — so the gap versus a true local link is only "must be online" and "doesn't show uncommitted edits." Second, the place where genuinely-local links are possible is the *runtime* surface, and it's already in the backlog: #51's OSC 8 idea. `vc-x1 config` knows the workspace root at print time, so it can emit terminal hyperlinks targeting `file:///<resolved-path>/vc-config.md` — machine-specific absoluteness is fine when it's computed at print time and never stored. If local-file linking matters, that's its home; the committed comment keeps the portable URL. A middle option exists (render a second plain-text line like `local: vc-config.md#anchor` as a human pointer, not a link), but I'd only add it if the URL alone proves insufficient — and note that choice *does* change rendered text, so it's a decide-before-regenerate item if wanted.

**On "next rung: add the vc-config.md file" — the design choice is where the copy comes from.** Two sources compete:

- **Baked into the binary** (`include_str!` at build time): init writes a `vc-config.md` that exactly matches the running binary's schema — the existing drift test already forces every key to anchor in it at build time, so binary and docs travel as one. No `--use-template` needed; a plain init gets docs too. Version skew between copy and binary is impossible *at creation*.
- **Copied from the template payload**: fits the pinned-family-file story (official copy in the payload, member diffs are proposals), but the payload's copy tracks convergence, not the binary the member runs, and init without a template has no source.

I lean baked-in: init's job is "create a workspace that matches this binary," and the family-pinning story can still layer on top — convergence updates the payload, members re-sync, and the payload copy is simply expected to match the current released binary. But it's exactly the kind of choice the rung's deliberation should record.

Your two-init observation also confirms something worth saying out loud: 0.78.7's generated output already lacked the `[push]` block — the fossil in the *committed* files predates it, which is why regenerating them is pure cleanup, and the only rendering delta the prototype pipeline introduced is the `reference:` line you saw.

On ordering: with the link answer above — committed file keeps the web URL — nothing about the init rung changes what regenerate renders, so regenerate stays unblocked and the init rung can sit after it (my earlier after-`--refresh` suggestion stands, though after-regenerate anywhere works). Only if you want the extra `local:` line does anything need to move in front.

The plain version: TOML comments can't do what markdown does — only real URLs are clickable, and committable-local isn't possible; the member-pointed web URL is the right stored form, and truly-local links belong to `vc-x1 config`'s printed output (the OSC 8 backlog item). The new rung's real question is whether init's `vc-config.md` comes baked from the binary (my lean — it can't skew) or copied from the payload, and unless we add a local-pointer line to the rendered block, regenerate doesn't need to wait for any of it.

content.text:
Thoughts, and I'll flag one wrinkle the example hides — the bot side's relative path — plus a placement consequence.

**The idea itself: sound, and the invented scheme is better than it first looks.** My earlier objection to local links was that nothing resolves them *by default*; your cw finding reframes it as progressive enhancement — the https line serves everyone unconditionally, and `localfile://` serves whoever teaches their editor one handler. An explicit made-up scheme is actually the right trigger for that: a custom handler can pattern-match `localfile://\S+` unambiguously, where a bare `./vc-config.md#anchor` is just text that's risky to auto-linkify. And unknown schemes degrade gracefully — GitHub's code view and terminals will show it as plain text, harmless. Zed lagging doesn't hurt: the https line is always there. Two nits on the form: URI-syntactically `localfile:./vc-config.md#anchor` (no `//`) is the correct shape for a scheme-relative path — `//` introduces an authority component, so `localfile://./...` parses as host `.` — but since only taught handlers will ever read it, pick whichever regexes cleaner and document it; and `references:` plural with `-` items costs two lines per key block, which reads fine to me given the file's whole job is self-documentation.

**The wrinkle: the localfile path is role-dependent, and the https one isn't.** The work repo's `.vc-config.toml` sits beside `vc-config.md`, so `./vc-config.md` is right. The bot repo's instance lives at `.claude/.vc-config.toml`, so *its* local reference is `../vc-config.md` — assuming the copy lives only at the work repo root, which I think is right (one copy per workspace, not per side). Today `render_key_block` is role-blind and shared by every surface (`config`'s printed schema, both init roles); a localfile line means threading the render context through, and deciding what the *printed* `vc-x1 config` output shows (it has a cwd, so it could resolve the real relative path at print time — or lean on backlog #51's OSC 8 and skip the question there). Not hard, but it's the actual design content of the change, and the example's single `./` form would be wrong in one of the two committed files.

**Placement: this goes in front of regenerate, as its own small rung.** It changes rendered text, so it's exactly the settle-the-generator-first case — and it's a renderer feature, which a `chore: regenerate` title shouldn't quietly contain (one title, one step's work). So the ladder would gain something like `feat: per-key references list (web + localfile)` immediately before the regenerate rung, and two records sync with it: acceptance item 1's "carry each key's `reference:` line" wording, and the drift tests (every key still needs its https entry; the localfile entry is derived from the same anchor, so the prototype needs no new per-key data). The insertion itself follows this cycle's precedent — recorded in deliberation rather than amending the pushed rungs' ladder snapshots.

The plain version: yes to `references:` with both lines — the web URL for everyone, the custom scheme for editors taught to handle it, and the scheme prefix is precisely what makes teaching them reliable. The one real design point is that the local path differs per side (`./` from the work repo, `../` from the bot repo), which means the renderer learns its render context. It should land as its own small feat rung ahead of the regenerate, with the acceptance wording and drift tests synced.

Want me to ladder it in — insert the rung, sync acceptance item 1, and note the insertion in deliberation?

1	# Todo
2	
3	This file contains near term tasks with a short description
4	and reference links to more details.
5	
6	Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
7	line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
8	pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.
9	
10	## In Progress
11	
12	A cycle's record has one home at a time, and while the cycle runs this is it. At Preparation
13	the picked-up `## Todo` item **moves** here (never copied, one home per text) and becomes six
14	provisional items, all required, all revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block moves
15	into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` and becomes that cycle's `##` section. It is never written in
16	two places. Shape:
17	
18	```
19	### <type>: <title>
20	
21	#### Problem
22	<what is wrong, a sentence or two>
23	
24	#### Solution
25	<what will be done about it, broad; provisional until the close-out>
26	
27	#### Acceptance check
28	<the measure of "are you finished?">
29	
30	#### Ladder
31	- <title> opening (done)
32	- <title> (current)
33	- <title>
34	- <close-out title>
35	
36	#### Deliberation
37	<how the five above were decided; `_None._` if there was nothing to deliberate>
38	
39	#### Ladder details
40	<optional: one `#####` subsection per rung with conceptual content, headed by its exact title>
41	```
42	
43	A multi-cycle program adds one level: the program is the `###`, its current cycle the `####`,
44	and the six items sit one level below that (headings give the current work durable anchors,
45	which numbered Todo entries can't). Full rules in
46	[cycle-protocol.md](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#preparation); the move's four transforms are
47	in [Chores sections](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).
48	
49	### docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd
50	
51	#### Problem
52	
53	Both repos' `.vc-config.toml` carry a fossil `[push]` comment block from an older binary's
54	schema, the retired `.vc-x1` state dirs linger (empty dirs on disk, a `/.vc-x1` line in the
55	work `.gitignore`), generated config comments have no refresh tooling so they rot silently, and
56	the bot dir's `.claude` name is agent-specific where this workspace wants the neutral
57	`.agent-session`.
58	
59	#### Solution
60	
61	Make a repo-root `vc-config.toml` prototype the schema's single source, then rebuild the
62	config surface from it:
63	
64	- the prototype holds real TOML tables, one per settable key: doc, used-by, default,
65	  reference url
66	- build.rs parses it and generates the schema table and default constants
67	  - `src/config_schema.rs` shrinks to the include plus hand-written helpers
68	  - behavioral defaults (col-width, result-lines) consume the generated constants, so the
69	    code cannot disagree with the file
70	- each key's rendered block carries a `doc references:` list: the derived web url plus a
71	  `localfile:` entry pointing at the workspace's own `vc-config.md` (relative path per side)
72	- regenerate both config files from that pipeline, retiring the fossil comment blocks
73	- retire the state-dir leftovers
74	- add a `config --refresh` that rewrites a file's commented schema block while preserving

Three things surfaced by the check, though — the first is a convention conflict you should rule on:

1. **The pinned convention says the opposite of what we now have.** cycle-protocol.md:180 — pinned by this very cycle's "docs: ladder ToC + per-rung sections" rung — says "No placeholder subsections: a rung with nothing to say has none," and this cycle's own deliberation records the same ("the subsection heading is conditional"). Two readings of your additions are compatible with intent deciding the file (hard rule 12): either they're *working scaffolding* — slots you want visible while the ladder runs, filled or deleted by each rung's completion, in which case the convention stands and nothing needs editing — or you now want *one section per rung always*, in which case the pinned wording in cycle-protocol.md (and prose.md's conditional-fourth-surface note, plus the two deliberation records here) should be amended as a family proposal, its own commit. Which is it?

2. **The close-out placeholder specifically collides.** "docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd" now heads both the cycle's `###` block and the new `#####` subsection — same text, colliding anchors in TODO.md, and after the close-out move it would collide with the chores `##` section header in the same file, which notes.md explicitly forbids. 3. **The grandfather note got captured.** The italic "_The program block below predates the six-item convention..._" line is a file-level note about the `### Refactor` program block beneath it, but the new empty close-out heading directly above now makes it read as that subsection's body. Dropping the close-out placeholder (point 2) fixes this too.

content.text:
I think you're right on both, and the close-out turns out to have an even cleaner answer than a suffix.

**Per-rung problem/solution: yes, with one guard.** The ladder-as-bare-ToC convention deliberately stripped rungs to titles, and the price is that a title alone under-describes a rung nobody has started yet. Your proposal completes the design: the ladder navigates, and each rung's subsection *describes* — opened when the rung is laddered with a sentence or two of intent (its problem and solution, provisional like everything in the block), then finished at completion with the conceptual delta as today. That also dissolves the placeholder question from last message: your new sections stop being empty placeholders and become intent stubs with content from birth, which the pinned "no placeholder subsections" rule was never aimed at — a stub with verbiage isn't a placeholder.

The guard: once a rung lands, its commit body states the final problem/solution, and the conventions rightly treat restating a commit body as the write-twice-drift shape. So the subsection's intent line should stay abstract-sized — a ToC-level summary, not a second commit body — and the completion edit keeps only what the body doesn't say.

**The collision: the opening already solves itself, and the close-out is exempt by construction.** As you note, the first rung carries the "opening" suffix, so it never collided. The colliding one was the close-out — but look at what its "problem and solution verbiage" would *be*: the cycle's own `#### Problem` and `#### Solution` items, sitting right above the ladder. The close-out rung *is* the cycle, so the block itself is its subsection. No `#####` needed, nothing duplicated, no collision possible. The bookends come out symmetric:

- opening rung: suffixed title, gets a subsection like any rung
- middle rungs: exact titles, each with an intent-stub subsection that completes at landing
- close-out rung: its intent is the block's Problem/Solution; its narrative becomes the chores section intro; no subsection

So the one edit to your additions: delete the empty `##### docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd` heading (which also frees the grandfather note trapped under it), and give the two remaining stubs their intent sentences.

**Where the rule lands**: this amends the pinned convention (cycle-protocol.md's Preparation wording, prose.md's conditional-fourth-surface note, notes.md's chores line), and an agent-file change is its own commit — so it's another inserted docs rung on this ladder, same species as "docs: separate work review stop". Something like `docs: rung subsections open with intent`, slotted before the doc-references rung so the convention lands before the rungs it governs.

Want me to ladder that in — insert the rung, drop the close-out placeholder, write intent stubs for the two empty sections, and record the insertion in deliberation?

content.text:
Thoughts — both halves have clean answers, and the second one has a precedent sitting in the conventions already.

**The `[[N]]` half: pre-shape the working ladder to the as-built form.** The chores as-built ladder already defines the rung form: literal `[[N]]` placeholder, backfilled with a real slot plus version once the commit's SHA is permanent. The working ladder in TODO.md could simply be born in that shape:

```
- [[N]] docs: separate work review stop (done)
- [[N]] docs: rung subsections open with intent (current)
```

One honest caveat: those placeholders will never fill *while in TODO.md*. Backfill waits for a permanent SHA, SHAs are unstable until the bookmark lands, and landing coincides with the close-out move — so during the cycle they stay literal. The value is uniformity, not early backfill: the close-out move stops re-shaping rungs (it just drops markers), and the ladder always looks like what it becomes.

**The local-reference half: linkify the title, exactly like the chores ToC.** The conventions already call the ladder "a bare table of contents," and the chores `## Table of Contents` already renders its entries as `- [<title>](#<anchor>)` — title-as-link, title text verbatim. The same idiom on rungs:

```
- [[N]] [feat: add config --refresh](#feat-add-config---refresh) (current)
```

- The title string stays verbatim inside the brackets, so hard rule 9's three-surface identity and grep-ability survive untouched.
- The links survive the close-out move for free: the subsections travel with the block into the same chores file, and heading slugs don't change with heading depth, so `#slug` keeps resolving.
- The close-out rung gets no link, consistent with its no-subsection exemption — its "section" is the block itself.
- The opening rung links fine: its "opening"-suffixed heading has its own slug.

**The known cost, and why now is still defensible**: this is the exact question the cycle declined earlier — hand-computed anchors are silently breakable. What changed is that `validate-anchors` is now two rungs away and its acceptance already covers TODO.md, so the unchecked window is short and then permanently guarded. We'd be adopting the convention slightly ahead of its checker, which the deliberation anticipated ("with anchors machine-checked, linking the ladder becomes nearly free").

**Where it lands**: this amends the pinned ladder-form wording (prose.md's ladder-step bullet and the shape templates in cycle-protocol, the checklists, and TODO.md's intro), so it's another its-own-commit docs rung — say `docs: ladder rungs carry refs and links` — slotted right after the current rung, which is sitting at its review stop uncommitted. I'd keep the two rungs separate: the current one changed what subsections *are*, this one changes what rungs *look like*, and one title covers one step.

The plain version: give every rung the chores-form `[[N]]` placeholder now (it fills only after landing, but the shape stops changing at the move), and make each rung's title a link to its subsection the way the chores ToC already links titles — close-out excepted since it has no subsection. Adopt it as its own docs rung right behind the one awaiting your review, accepting a two-rung window where the links are hand-checked until validate-anchors lands and guards them.

content.text:
Both halves of that are real findings. Taking them in turn.

**Yes — the table can carry local links, and routing the ladder's links through it kills the noise.** A `[N]:` definition's destination can be any link destination, including a bare fragment like `#feat-add-config---refresh`. Markdown's reference-style links then let the rung cite it instead of embedding it:

```
- [[N]] [feat: add config --refresh][12] (current)

[12]: #feat-add-config---refresh
```

The rung line shrinks to the title in brackets plus a two-or-three-character tag, the slug moves to the `# References` table where long tokens already live, and the machinery is all existing house machinery: file-local numbers, re-packable, and the close-out move's renumber-into-destination transform already handles exactly this. The fragments survive the move untouched since the subsections travel to the same file. Two variants considered and set aside:

- Shortcut form `[<title>]` with a title-text definition is the cleanest inline, but a title edit silently breaks it (the label stops matching and the link degrades to bracketed text), where a numbered tag survives title syncs.
- A trailing citation (`<title> [[12]]`) keeps the title barest of all, but makes the reader click a number instead of the title, and adds a second bracket blob anyway.

So my recommendation: revise the rung form to `- [[N]] [<title>][M] (marker)` with `[M]: #<slug>` definitions in the file's `# References`. The just-finished rung is still uncommitted at its review stop, so this is a cheap revision to it, not a new rung — same convention, better syntax.

**The `/notes/forks-multi-user.md` observation: those definitions are house pointers, not working links, and your VS Code experience is the symptom.** A leading-slash destination is site-absolute in rendered markdown — on GitHub it resolves to `github.com/notes/...`, a 404, not the repo file. VS Code's preview is more forgiving and resolves `/` against the workspace root, which is why it "kinda works" there; the scroll-to-bottom blank screen we think is VS Code's preview failing to find a fragment to land on (those defs carry no `#anchor`) and botching the scroll position — speculation, not measured. The genuinely portable form is a relative path with an anchor (`notes/forks-multi-user.md#...` from a repo-root file), which both GitHub and VS Code resolve. That's a change to the reference-path convention in notes.md plus a sweep of existing defs — and cross-file targets are precisely what `validate-anchors` could grow to check. I'd record it as a backlog entry (or fold into validate-anchors' rung intent as a stretch check) rather than swallow it into the current rung.

Want me to (a) revise the uncommitted rung to the table-routed form — ladder, template, and the four pinned files' form wording — and (b) add the relative-paths follow-up to the backlog?

Thoughts — agreed on the substance: rule 13 says `main` advances only by landing a cycle, the first three rungs advancing it mid-cycle was the deviation, and moving `main` back to 73319b8c ("docs: consolidate line widths", 0.78.7) restores the invariant. Four consequences to handle, one of which bites something we did minutes ago:

- **The backfill I just did becomes premature.** The timing rule is explicit — never record a SHA that is not on a permanent branch — and moving `main` back takes 91ebbae3, b02741a4, and 8143157d off the permanent branch. They become draft commits that the drafts rule explicitly permits rewriting, which is precisely what the rule guards against: an amend mid-cycle would falsify the recorded SHAs. So the consistent move is to revert the three rungs to bare `[[N]]` (and drop defs `[44]`-`[46]`), letting the close-out's backfill step refill them at landing. If the trapezoid preserves the series unrewritten, the same SHAs come back; the revert costs nothing but honesty about when they're safe to write. The versions leave with the SHAs (the rule ties them together deliberately).

- **The bot repo mirrors the problem.** Its `main` presumably advanced in step with the work side's pushes. The paired bot commit for 73319b8c is findable via the `ochid:` trailers, and the same backward move applies there. To check when we act.

- **The remote legs are backward moves of published `main`.** Nothing is lost — every commit stays reachable through the pushed `config-refresh` bookmark — but it's a forced update of a published ref on both sides, so it's exactly the class of op that waits for your explicit go at the moment of doing it.

content.text:
Thoughts — your instinct is right, and the interesting part is *where* the limits come from: not from jj, which happily does all that surgery on a draft line, but from the two things this project welds onto commits — ochid pairing and the bot repo's nature as a log.

**What survives surgery cleanly.** The pairing is by jj change id, which is exactly the identifier built to survive rewrites. So on the draft line:

- content amends into any rung: pair intact, trailer rides along
- rebasing the whole series (e.g., onto a corrected `main`): pairs intact
- reordering rungs: pairs intact — the pairing is per-commit, not per-position, so the two repos' orders diverging is cosmetic
- ladder/TODO snapshot edits plus force-push, per the drafts rule, under push approval

**Where the dual repo bites.** Each of the remaining operations is one-sided in a way single-repo jj never is:

- **Delete a rung**: the bot counterpart now carries an `ochid:` pointing at an abandoned change — a dangling ref. Mirroring the delete means destroying session history, which is the one thing the bot repo exists to keep. So deletion is really "keep the bot commit, accept the dangling pointer, note why" — a coordinated act, not a casual `jj abandon`.
- **Insert or split**: new commits minted mid-series have no trailer and can't get one — rule 5 says only `vc-x1 push` stamps, and it stamps at the tip when it commits, not retroactively mid-history. An inserted commit is permanently unpaired unless the series is reshaped so it arrives through a push.
- **Merge two rungs**: the squash concatenates or drops descriptions, which is rule 4 territory (trailer-carrying descriptions), and the survivor ends up claiming two bot counterparts or orphaning one.
- **Anything touching a description**: rule 4 regardless of shape.

**And one timing limit**: the trapezoid close-out (as we understand it — `jj git push` at its step 4, no restamp) lands the series *as it stands*. So surgery freedom decays over the cycle: widest just after moving `main` back, gone once the close-out shape is being assembled — and any rewrite between backfill and landing is exactly what the SHA-timing rule protects against, which is why the backfill revert we discussed belongs with the `main` move.

The underlying asymmetry is worth saying once: the work repo is an *artifact* — drafts are meant to be reshaped; the bot repo is a *log* — its value is that nobody reshapes it. The ochid weld between them tolerates rewrites (change ids) but not identity changes (delete, split, merge). So the practical rule of thumb: operations that keep every rung's identity are free; operations that create or destroy rung identities need coordination and mostly want to be done *before* a rung is pushed, not after.

The plain version: yes — amend, rebase, and reorder stay safe even dual-repo, because the cross-repo links track changes, not SHAs or positions. Deleting, splitting, merging, or inserting commits breaks or starves the pairing on one side, so those want deliberate coordination, and ideally happen before a rung ever publishes. The freedom is real but front-loaded in the cycle, and it never extends to descriptions.

What's ad hoc today is the *name*: `config-refresh` was an invented shorthand, and the bookmark list shows the pattern at scale (`line-widths`, `agents-semicolons`, `adopt-agent-files`... each a naming decision someone made). content.text:
This is worth getting structurally right, because the two concerns pull at different levels — and I think the answer is one preamble sentence, not per-rule exception clauses.

**First, a reframe that dissolves part of the tension**: the hard rules bind *the bot*. When you historically pushed a simple change straight to `main` from your terminal, no rule was violated — they're instructions to the agent, and the human is the authority the rules answer to. So rule 13 doesn't need to license your own behavior; it needs to govern mine, plus say what the *cycle machinery* assumes.

**For emergencies and simple changes, the system already has the release valve**: rule 10's stop-and-ask. An exception the user grants explicitly at the moment is fine under every rule — that's just the user steering. What must never happen is the bot *self-granting* an exception under time pressure, which is precisely the failure mode hard rules exist to block. An "emergency" doesn't change this: the user is the one who declares the emergency, so the user is right there to say "push it straight to main, skip the cycle."

**So my recommendation**: keep the redrafted rule 13 clean as agreed, and add one sentence to the `## Hard rules` preamble in AGENTS.md, covering all thirteen at once:

> The rules bind the bot, and none is absolute: any rule bends when wink says so explicitly at the moment (rule 10's stop-and-ask is the path), and a taken exception is recorded in the cycle's records. No rule bends silently, and no exception is self-granted.

Why preamble over per-rule clauses: each rule stays terse and absolute-sounding — the right default posture for an agent reading it mid-task — while the exception mechanism lives in one place with its two guardrails attached (user-granted, recorded). Scattering "unless it's an emergency" through individual rules invites exactly the creative self-exemption the guardrails prevent.

One residual note for the shared-repo case you raised: when the family's repos gain multiple humans, "nobody pushes straight to main" becomes *repo policy* (branch protection) rather than agent instruction — a different enforcement layer, worth a line in the checklists' bookmark section rather than in the hard rule.

If this sits right, I'll add both to the rung's intent stub — the agreed rule 13 text verbatim, and the preamble sentence — so the drafting is locked in for when the rung runs.

message.content: But even "The rules bind the bot" isn't absolute, because there have been few times, I've asked you to complete a mult-step cycle on your own, in which case you don't need the typcial approval cycle. Someday I expect you'll do complete projects on your own. But I still expect you to follow our flow. How do you think we should have situations such as that?

content.text:
The distinction that I think resolves this — including the someday-full-projects case — is between the **flow** and the **stops**. They're different kinds of thing, and delegation should only ever touch one of them.

The *flow* is the protocol's structure: cycles with openings and closings, rungs on a bookmark, records written as work lands (ladder, deliberation, chores), validation before every push, titles lining up across their surfaces. The *stops* are the synchronous gates where I wait for you: work review, description review, push approval. When you say "complete this cycle on your own," you're waiving stops. The flow you still expect — and that's not a preference quirk, it's load-bearing: **the records are what convert real-time supervision into after-the-fact review.** A delegated cycle with full records is completely reviewable when you return; a delegated cycle that skipped the flow is just unsupervised work. The stops and the records are two implementations of the same review, one synchronous, one deferred — which is why delegation can waive one only because the other remains.

That framing gives delegation natural tiers, and the bookmark discipline we just fixed is precisely what makes the middle tier safe:

- **Interactive** (default): every stop, as today.
- **Delegated cycle**: you name the task and the scope; rungs push to the topic bookmark without per-push asks; all records still written; validation never waived; destructive and irreversible ops still pause regardless. `main` is untouched by construction — the bookmark is the containment vessel — so your review moves to the end: read the line, then land it. The hard stop compresses to the turn's final push.
- **Delegated project** (the someday case): landing too is delegated; your review happens after landing, and corrections become new cycles. Same flow, review deferred one notch further.

The rules half-anticipate this already — "only an explicit scoped delegation waives the stops," "a standing delegation makes intermediate pushes just steps" — but as scattered carve-outs on rules 2 and 3, not as a stated doctrine. I'd formalize it in two small pieces:

1. The preamble sentence we drafted grows one clause: a rule bends when you say so *at the moment, or in advance as an explicit scoped delegation* — still never self-granted, still recorded.
2. A short passage in the protocol's Pushing policy stating the doctrine: **delegation waives stops, never flow** — records, validation, and the bookmark discipline are invariant because they're what deferred review reads; destructive ops pause in every tier; landing is its own tier, delegated separately.

That second piece is its own concern, and the current rung's title is already carrying two — so my lean is a separate tiny rung, `docs: delegation waives stops, not flow`, right behind the bookmark one. The phrase is the rule; a rung title you can quote is worth having.

The plain version: the way to have those situations is to make delegation a first-class mode rather than a rule-bend — you grant it explicitly and scoped, it removes the waiting-for-you gates but never the record-keeping, and the untouched `main` plus the full records mean you review everything after the fact instead of during. Autonomy scales by deferring review, never by skipping what review reads.

Want me to ladder that rung in with the two drafts recorded in its stub?

content.text:
Thoughts — and the diagnosis has two layers worth separating, because one is fixable in place and the other needs a rule.

**Layer one: the deliberation is bloated because I've been writing rung-sized narrative into it.** Every insertion got a multi-bullet saga. But the convention we just adopted says exactly where rung verbiage belongs: the rung's own stub. Deliberation's job is "how the six items were decided" — an insertion deserves one line ("rung X inserted at Y's review, see its stub"), with the story living in the stub the ladder already links to. So the immediate fix needs no restructuring at all: collapse each convention bullet to a one-liner pointing at its rung's subsection, moving any narrative not already there into the stub. Nothing is lost, and the deliberation returns to being a list of decisions instead of a chronicle. That's mechanical and I can do it in this block today.

**Layer two: you're right about the place.** This cycle's title promises vc-config work, and of its rungs, four are now convention amendments — the review stop, the ladder ToC, and the two queued ones, plus the open one. Convention work kept riding this cycle because each change was discovered mid-flight and inserting a rung was cheap. The rule that prevents recurrence is simple and belongs in the pinned set: **agent-file convention work runs as its own cycle, never as insertions into a feature cycle** — a mid-feature convention itch becomes a backlog entry or a small dedicated cycle between features. The bloat we're looking at is the motivating exhibit, and the "define cycle" rung is the natural place to pin that rule since it's already defining what a cycle is.

**What I'd *not* do: extract the queued convention rungs into a separate cycle now.** I checked the dependency and it's unfavorable — the uncommitted convention edits textually build on the ladder-ToC rung's edits to the same pinned files, which are on this cycle's bookmark, so a conventions cycle would have to stack on `config-refresh` and couldn't land until this cycle's pushed rungs land anyway. Stacked bookmarks are the drafts rule's own listed headache. Extraction buys clean history at the cost of real mechanics, on a cycle whose mixing is already committed history four rungs deep. Better to finish this cycle as the grandfathered mixed exhibit, readable via the deliberation diet, with the rule ensuring it's the last of its kind.

So the rectification I'd propose: (1) diet this block's deliberation now — one line per decision, narrative into stubs; (2) add the conventions-get-their-own-cycle rule to the "define cycle + bookmark discipline" rung's intent; (3) run the two queued docs rungs as planned and then stay feature-only for the rest of the ladder.

The plain version: the mess is half writing style, half placement. The style fix is to let deliberation hold decisions in one line each and push the stories into the rung stubs, which the new convention already prescribes. The placement fix is a new rule — convention changes get their own small cycles from now on — rather than surgery on this one, because the queued convention work is textually stacked on this cycle's own commits and extracting it costs more than finishing it. Want me to do the diet and add the rule?

## Cycle bookmarks: create and land

The mechanics behind
[Cycles run on a bookmark](cycle-checklists.md#cycles-run-on-a-bookmark). That section holds
the rule and when it applies; this one holds the commands.

**Create**, at the cycle's opening, with the bookmark named for the cycle rather than the step:

- `jj git push --named <bookmark>=@- -R .` is the common case: it creates the bookmark at the
  last committed change and publishes it in one invocation.
- Any other revision works as the `=<rev>` right-hand side. When `<rev>` is not `@-`, follow with
  `jj new <rev> -R .` so the working copy actually sits on the new line. Otherwise the bookmark
  exists and the next commit lands somewhere else.
- `jj bookmark set <bookmark> -r <rev> -R .` creates it without publishing, for a line that is
  not ready to be seen.

**Land**, once the close-out is approved: fast-forward the permanent branch to the bookmark.

- `jj bookmark set main -r <bookmark> -R .`, then `jj git push --bookmark main -R .`.
- It is a fast-forward, so `--allow-backwards` is not wanted. Needing it means the bookmark is
  not a descendant of `main`, and the situation wants a look, not a flag.
- Landing is the moment the cycle's commits become permanent, so it triggers the records that
  wait on permanence: the chores as-built rungs take their SHAs and versions
  ([Chores commit references](notes.md#chores-commit-references)).
- The bookmark is redundant once landed and may be deleted (`jj bookmark delete <bookmark>`),
  the same disposal the long-lived case gets below.

We think a `vc-x1 start-change <bookmark>` will eventually own the create half. It would replace
the create bullets and nothing else, which is why the rule and the commands are separated.

## Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged

A long-lived bookmark (a program line pushed rung by rung across cycles) is not a cycle bookmark:
it carries published history, and the discipline protects that history while the bookmark is its
only holder.

- conflicts with `main` are resolved in merge commits, never by rewriting published rungs
- a rebase is never required for correctness: it is a linearity preference
- coordinated rebases stay available (the bar is on unilateral rewrites, not rewrites), at the
  known cost of staling the git-SHA citations in the records. Chids and ochid trailers survive
  a rebase
- once the bookmark's history is fully merged into `main` the bookmark is redundant and may be
  deleted

The contrast with a cycle bookmark is the whole point: that one is a draft and may be rewritten

phases always happen, but there are two styles. A **multi-step** cycle commits them
