**Delegation waives stops, never flow.** The stops (work review, description review, per-push
approval, the hard stop after the final push) are the synchronous half of review. The flow
(the records, the validation, the bookmark discipline) is what deferred review reads, so no
delegation waives it: a delegated cycle writes every record and validates every commit exactly
as an interactive one, and the user reviews after the fact what they would otherwise have
reviewed in real time. The tiers:

- **Interactive** (the default): every stop, as above.
- **Delegated cycle**: rungs push to the topic bookmark without per-push asks; `main` is
  untouched by construction, so review happens at landing: read the line, then land it.
- **Delegated project**: landing is delegated too; review happens after, and corrections
  become new cycles.

Destructive ops pause in every tier, and landing is its own tier, delegated separately.

Thoughts — I like it, and it's cleaner than the exemption we just pinned, but it pulls one thread that should be pulled deliberately: the suffix has to go on the *commit title itself*, not just the subsection heading.

**Why the commit title is implicated.** The opening's " opening" suffix works because it's genuinely the opening commit's title — rule 9's identity (ladder rung = chores header = commit title) holds. If the closing rung's subsection is headed "<title> closing" but the commit stays bare, the three-surface identity breaks for exactly one rung. So the proposal really is: the multi-step close-out commit becomes `<cycle title> closing`. That's a change to the bookend convention, and it actually *improves* it: the bare cycle title becomes the cycle's name — carried by the chores `##` header and the TODO `###` heading, matched by no commit — while `git log --grep "<cycle title>"` returns the two suffixed bookends bracketing the ladder. Symmetric, and the anchor collision dissolves because the section header and the closing subsection now have different slugs by construction.

**One nuance: single-step cycles keep the bare title.** Their one commit *is* the cycle, there's no ladder to bracket, no subsections exist (the block folds), so no suffix and no collision. The suffixes are ladder bookends, not cycle decoration.

**On the gotchas rule, my reading of your exception**: the closing rung's subsection has no intent beat — its problem/solution is the block's own Problem and Solution items, so writing an intent stub would duplicate them — and it exists *only when gotchas occurred*: acceptance-check surprises, validation trip-ups, close-out-move wrinkles, anything learned while closing that the commit body's broad problem/solution shouldn't carry. No gotchas, no subsection — which also means the closing rung's ladder link is added at close-out, when and if the subsection is created (that's already the last-edit-sync moment, so no new mechanics). The chores section intro keeps the cycle narrative; the closing subsection holds specifically what closing taught.

So the closing rung becomes: suffixed title always, subsection and link conditional on gotchas, intent never. The rest of the convention is untouched.

**Cost accounting is favorable right now**: the "close-out rung has no subsection" wording we just pinned lives entirely in the *uncommitted* rung's diff — cycle-protocol's Preparation paragraph, rule 13 untouched, prose.md's bookends and fourth-surface notes, notes.md's collision warning, the checklists, the TODO template, and this cycle's own last rung (which would become `docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd closing`). Folding this in before the rung publishes costs a revision pass; adopting it a cycle later would cost a second convention commit. This is exactly what the review stop is for.

The plain version: yes — but it means the closing commit is really titled "<cycle title> closing" (multi-step only; single-step stays bare), the bare title becomes the cycle's name carried by the section header, and the closing subsection is gotchas-only: no intent stub, created at close-out only if there's something to confess, its ladder link arriving with it. All of it folds into the open uncommitted rung. Two things to confirm before I revise: the suffix on the actual commit title, and gotchas-conditional rather than always-present.

They're deliberately not — both were parked in the backlog as seeds for their own cycles, and each stub that touches them points outward ("beyond this cycle: backlog #52" in the regenerate and doc-references stubs; "stretch, from backlog #53" in the validate-anchors stub). The reasoning, worth restating since it was spread over several exchanges:

**#52 (init distributes vc-config.md, reference-base stamped per member)** is close to cycle-sized on its own: it carries an unsolved design problem (the member's repo URL usually doesn't exist yet at init time — stamping `reference-base` needs an answer), plus template-payload seeding and existing-member migration, which are cross-repo work beyond a vc-x1 rung. This cycle already has seven rungs still to run against an acceptance check that says nothing about init. What this cycle *does* deliver toward it is the doc-references machinery those seeded copies will be linked by.

**#53 (relative reference defs)** got strengthened by something we did *today*: its heart is a notes.md convention change (the `[N]:` path form) plus a repo-wide sweep of existing defs — and the conventions-own-cycle rule this open rung is about to publish says exactly that work gets its own small cycle, never rides a feature ladder. Pulling #53 in would violate the rule in the same commit that creates it. The validate-anchors rung keeps the cross-file check as a named stretch, but it builds the same-file checks first either way.

So the intended shape: this cycle finishes its config work; #52 opens as the next feature cycle with a full seed already written; #53 opens as a small conventions cycle under the new rule. Both backlog entries were written dense enough that their openings cost little.

That said, it's your ladder — if you want #52's init work in this cycle after all, it slots after `config --refresh` per the earlier ordering argument, and the acceptance check would need a matching item (a deliberation-worthy change). #53 I'd genuinely hold out, for the rule-consistency reason above. They are related — your instinct is right, and the confusion is just about which half each one owns. The seam:

- **The doc-references rung** is the *rendering* side: the renderer in this repo learns to emit the `doc references:` block you pasted — the derived web URL and the `localfile://` entry — into any `.vc-config.toml` it renders. It delivers your example in this workspace, this cycle: both of vc-x1's own config files get working links, because vc-x1's repo actually contains `vc-config.md` and has `reference-base` pointing at itself.

- **Backlog #52** is the *distribution* side: making those same links work in everyone else's repos. A member like iiac-perf has no `vc-config.md` copy and no member-pointed `reference-base`, so #52 is what seeds the copy at init and stamps the URL — turning the links the rung renders into links that land on a file the member owns.

So the rung builds the pointers; #52 builds what they point at, everywhere that isn't vc-x1. The rung doesn't depend on #52; #52 consumes the rung's work.

And explaining this surfaced a genuine coupling worth recording: `init` writes new configs through this same renderer, so once the rung lands, a plain `vc-x1 init` produces a config whose `localfile://` entries point at a `vc-config.md` that init doesn't yet create — dangling in fresh members until #52 lands (or init suppresses the localfile line in the interim, a choice for #52's design). That's precisely why the two feel like one thing: #52 is the natural next cycle after this one. Recording the coupling in both places:

message.content: So .vc-config.toml in vc-x1 will have it but it won't be emitted by `vc-x1 init xxx`?

content.text:
Not quite — init *will* emit it. Both init and this repo's regenerate go through the same renderer, so after the doc-references rung lands, `vc-x1 init xxx` writes config files carrying the full `doc references:` block, same as vc-x1's own. The difference is in what the two entries *resolve to* in a fresh member, before #52:

- **The web entry works everywhere.** `reference-base` defaults to vc-x1's repo URL, so a fresh member's web links point at vc-x1's hosted `vc-config.md` — reachable, correct docs. What #52 changes is *where* it points: to the member's own copy instead.
- **The localfile entry is the dangler.** Init emits `localfile://./vc-config.md#...` but doesn't create `vc-config.md` in the new repo — nothing puts that file there until #52's seeding. So in a fresh member, the local link points at a file that doesn't exist; in vc-x1's own repos it resolves, because this repo carries the file.

So the state after this cycle, before #52: every rendered config has the full block; web links work everywhere; localfile links work in vc-x1 and dangle in fresh members. The recorded design call for closing that gap belongs to #52, with two candidate shapes: seed the file (the real fix), or have init suppress the localfile line until it can seed (the interim politeness). A third option exists at the renderer level — emit the localfile entry only when the target file exists at render time — which the doc-references rung could adopt if you'd rather no dangling link ever ships; it costs a bit of context plumbing but makes the rendering honest by construction.

The plain version: init does emit the block; the web link always works; only the local-file link is ahead of its file in fresh members until #52 seeds copies — and if even a temporary dangle bothers you, the rung can make the localfile line conditional on the file existing.

content.text:
Yes, by default — with the anchor varying per key, and with one knob that changes it.

The URL is derived at render time as `reference-base` + `/blob/HEAD/vc-config.md` + the key's anchor. `reference-base` is a settable key whose *built-in default* is vc-x1's repo URL, baked into the binary from the prototype. So any workspace that hasn't set `reference-base` — which today is every workspace — renders exactly that vc-x1-pointing link family. That's coherent for now: vc-x1's `vc-config.md` is the tool's canonical documentation, and pointing everyone's configs at the canonical copy is a sensible default for a binary that documents itself.

What changes it is setting `reference-base` in a workspace's own `.vc-config.toml` — an active key, preserved by every refresh — after which all that workspace's links derive from the new base. That's precisely the knob #52 has init stamp with the member's own URL, flipping members from "read the canonical docs at vc-x1" to "read (and propose edits to) your own carried copy."

Two caveats worth having in view:

- **Skew**: a member running an older binary still gets links into vc-x1's *HEAD* docs, which may describe a newer schema than the binary they run. `/blob/HEAD/` was chosen deliberately (no branch baked in), so this is accepted, not accidental.
- **The bare default only fits repos vc-x1 knows about.** An outside adopter's config points at winksaville's repo until they set the key — fine for docs-reading, and the fork guidance (customize base + file together) covers the rest.

The plain version: yes — every config rendered with an unset `reference-base` carries vc-x1-pointing links like your example, today including fresh members. Setting the key repoints a whole workspace's links at once, and stamping it per member at init is exactly the #52 work.

52. **init distributes vc-config.md; reference-base points at the member** (wink + bot,
    2026-08-10). `vc-x1 init` seeds a new member with a copy of `vc-config.md` from the
    template payload and stamps `[vc-config] reference-base` with the member's own repo url,
    so every generated doc-reference web link in the member's `.vc-config.toml` lands on a
    copy the member owns. The copy is a pinned family file: a member's edits diff against the payload
    and are its doc proposals, folded back at convergence.
    - the instance `.vc-config.toml` stays the only behavior-changing file: pinning and
      value-carrying are mutually exclusive, since workspace values in a pinned copy would
      pollute the diff-as-proposal property
    - the prototype `vc-config.toml` stays vc-x1-only build source (schema proposals travel by
      family channel or fork), and workspace-local keys wait on the `[private]` table
    - `validate-anchors` gains member-side work: the carried copy must still have the headings
      the instance's `reference:` links anchor at
    - settled at the "chore: regenerate stale config files" rung of the "docs: freshen
      vc-config and config subcmd" cycle; the fuller ownership model is recorded there
    - the `localfile://./vc-config.md#<anchor>` entry in each key's `doc references:` list
      lands here, not in the doc-references rung it was drafted in (cut at review, wink
      2026-08-10): the entry is useless until the file it names exists locally, which is
      this entry's seeding. Editors and terminals need a taught handler for the scheme
      (claude-web: straightforward in neovim / vscode, harder in zed); the rendered list
      form already leaves room, so adding the entry is append-only

content.text:
Short answer: it's not GitHub-*only*, but it is a convention, not a standard. Markdown itself (CommonMark) defines link syntax and says nothing about how a viewer resolves paths. What each viewer does with `/notes/foo.md`:

- **GitHub** (and GitLab similarly) rewrite links in rendered repo files, resolving a leading `/` against the *repository root* — a forge convention.
- **VS Code**'s preview resolves a leading `/` against the *workspace root* — an IDE convention that happens to align. (The weak "back" is a known preview limitation — its navigation history is shallow — and no path form we choose can fix that.)
- **Zed** and most filesystem-based viewers do the literal thing: `/notes/...` is an absolute filesystem path, which doesn't exist. Dead link.

The only form with universal behavior is the **file-relative path** (`forks-multi-user.md` from a sibling, `../notes/...` from elsewhere): every link-resolving viewer resolves relative to the containing file, because that's the one interpretation that needs no convention. So your Zed measurement swings #53 back toward its original direction — relative paths plus anchors — but now for the measured reason, not my refuted one: the `/` form is a GitHub/VS Code convention that filesystem viewers don't share. The costs stay real (a notes.md convention change, a def sweep, and refs becoming location-dependent — though the close-out move's transform list already handles relative-link rewrites, and this cycle's validate-anchors is the machinery that keeps a sweep honest). Under the new conventions-own-cycle rule it stays a small dedicated cycle.

| `TODO.md` (root) | `notes/forks-multi-user.md` |
| `notes/chores/chores-16.md` | `../forks-multi-user.md` |

message.content: No I mean from a "standards" PoV

content.text:
Yes — in the standards sense, the relative form is the canonical one, and the chain is worth spelling out:

- **CommonMark** defines only the link *syntax*. A destination is just a string that becomes an `href`; the spec deliberately says nothing about resolution. So "what does this path mean" was never markdown's question.
- **RFC 3986 (URI syntax) and the WHATWG URL Standard** are where resolution actually lives. They define *relative references* and the exact algorithm for resolving one against a base URI — the base being the containing document's own URI. `forks-multi-user.md`, `./forks-multi-user.md`, and `../<file>.md` are all standard relative-path references, and the dot-segments (`.` and `..`) have precisely specified normalization (RFC 3986's `remove_dot_segments`). Any conforming resolver — browser, IDE, forge — produces the identical answer with no special-casing. That's *why* they work everywhere: universality is the standard doing its job.
- The **`/notes/...` form is also standard syntax** (an "absolute-path reference"), but the standard resolves it against the base's *root* — and per the plain algorithm, on a GitHub page whose URL is `github.com/owner/repo/blob/HEAD/notes/todo-backlog.md`, `/notes/x` resolves to `github.com/notes/x`. GitHub *rewrites* those links to the repo root instead — a deliberate nonstandard courtesy, which is exactly the convention layer we measured. VS Code does its own version (workspace root); Zed does the unadorned standard-adjacent thing for a local file (filesystem root) and the link dies. The divergence lives entirely in "what is the root," which the standard leaves to the host.

On `./x.md` versus bare `x.md`: the standards treat them as equivalent (normalization removes the `./`), so neither is more canonical — `./` is just the explicit spelling, plus one edge the grammar cares about: a first segment containing a colon (`foo:bar.md`) would parse as a URI scheme, and the `./` prefix forces path interpretation. Choosing `./` as house style is a stylistic call the standard is indifferent to.

The plain version: yes — relative-with-dot-segments is the form the URL standards define end-to-end, which is why every viewer agrees on it; the leading-slash form is standard *syntax* whose *meaning* each host invents, which is why they disagreed.

content.text:
The description for review:

---

**Title:**

```
docs: amend cycle conventions
```

**Body:**

```
The cycle conventions had gaps this cycle kept hitting live. A bare-title ladder
under-described rungs nobody had started and linked to nothing. The word "cycle" carried half
the hard rules without a definition. Rule 13 read poorly and was ambiguous about which repo
the bookmark discipline governs, and this cycle's first three rungs advanced main mid-cycle
under that ambiguity. Bookmark names were ad hoc, landed bookmarks accumulated undeleted,
exceptions and delegation existed only as scattered carve-outs, and what a close-out learns
had no anchored home.

The pinned set is amended in one conventions commit, deliberately the last of its kind:
convention work runs as its own cycle from here on. Rung subsections run in two beats, an
intent stub at laddering and the conceptual delta at landing. The ladder becomes a linked
table of contents: each rung carries the as-built [[N]] placeholder and its title links to
its subsection through the file's references table. AGENTS.md gains a Terminology entry for
the cycle (three stages, folded into one commit single-step or laddered multi-step) and a
preamble sentence: no rule bends silently, no exception is self-granted. Rule 13 now says a
cycle runs on one work-repo bookmark named by the cycle title's slug, that main advances only
by landing a finished cycle, and that a landed bookmark is deleted locally and remotely; the
bot repo's main rides the tip of its linear narrative. Multi-step bookend commits are
"<cycle title> opening" and "<cycle title> closing", with the closing rung's subsection
existing only for gotchas, in problem/solution form. Delegation is a mode rather than a bend:
it waives the stops, never the flow that deferred review reads. Riders: this cycle's bookmark
renamed to the title-slug form, and landed straggler bookmarks swept.
```

---

For clarity on what a go here covers: approving this description is not yet the push. The pushes queued after your approval are (1) `vc-x1 push docs-freshen-vc-config-and-config-subcmd --title ... --body ...` for the rung itself, then the bookmark bookkeeping legs: (2) push the renamed bookmark and delete remote `config-refresh`, (3) delete the three swept remote refs (`line-widths`, `agents-semicolons`, `config-discoverability`), and (4) your still-open call on `adopt-agent-files`' diverged remote ref. Each waits for its own go.

Thoughts — you've spotted my draft violating the records' own division of labor. The conventions say the three records don't restate each other: the diff is the mechanical record, the *body* is problem/solution broad, and the design thinking lives in chores. My solution paragraph restated the rung subsection nearly bullet for bullet — the write-twice shape. So the fix isn't just shortening; it's putting the detail's *one* home back in the subsection and letting the body be genuinely broad.

On "reference the section": the system already solved the moving-target problem, and it's why hard rule 9 exists — **the reference is the title, not a link**. The subsection is headed by this commit's exact title, in TODO.md today and in the cycle's chores section after the close-out move; `git log --grep` one way, `grep -r "docs: amend cycle conventions"` the other, and the pointer survives the move because titles are the durable identifiers where paths and anchors are not. So the body can say "the design record is this title's rung subsection" without naming a file at all.

**Title:**

```
docs: amend cycle conventions
```

**Body:**

```
The cycle conventions had gaps this cycle kept hitting live:

- a bare-title ladder under-described unstarted rungs and linked to nothing
- "cycle" carried hard rules without a definition, and rule 13 was ambiguous about which
  repo the bookmark discipline governs (three rungs advanced main mid-cycle under it)
- bookmark names were ad hoc, and landed bookmarks lingered undeleted
- exceptions and delegation existed only as scattered carve-outs
- what a close-out learns had no anchored home

Amend the pinned set in one conventions commit: two-beat rung subsections, the ladder as a
linked table of contents, a cycle definition and exceptions preamble in AGENTS.md, rule 13
rewritten, suffixed cycle bookends with a gotchas-only closing subsection, and delegation as
a mode that waives stops, never flow. Convention work runs as its own cycle from here on.
The design record is this title's rung subsection, in TODO.md until close-out moves it to
chores.
```

---

The solution names each amendment in two or three words and stops — anyone needing the *content* of an amendment greps the title. If even that list feels heavy, the floor I'd defend is keeping "rule 13 rewritten" and "delegation as a mode" visible, since those two change behavior most; but I think seven half-lines is the right altitude for a commit this wide.
